questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with a nonhealing diabetic foot ulcer and osteomyelitis is alert and oriented. After the surgeon explains the risks of declining, the client says he does not want a below-knee amputation. As the surgeon leaves, she tells the nurse, “See if you can talk some sense into him.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Tell the client that most people in his situation choose to have surgery
Ask the client to describe what could happen if he declines the surgery
Call the client’s wife and ask her to help him reconsider his decision
Have the client sign an informed refusal form before the surgeon leaves
optionRationales: Incorrect. Comparing him with others is pressure; it expresses disapproval instead of confirming an informed choice.
Correct. Assessing his understanding shows whether the refusal is informed and whether the surgeon needs to explain more.
Incorrect. Recruiting family to change a capable adult’s mind is paternalism and bypasses his autonomy.
Incorrect. Documenting the refusal is appropriate later, but it skips confirming that the refusal is informed.
questions.rationale: A capable adult may refuse treatment, but the refusal must be informed. Before documenting or acting, the nurse first assesses whether the client understands the consequences, which also shows whether the surgeon needs to explain more. The surgeon’s request to “talk sense” into him invites paternalism; the nurse’s role is to stay objective, not to persuade. Having him sign a refusal form is tempting because it feels like respecting his choice, but it skips confirming that the choice is informed.
questions.takeaway: Before honoring or documenting a refusal, confirm the client understands the consequences, then respect the choice without persuading.
questions.hintContent: A refusal is only as valid as the client’s understanding of what refusing means.
questions.hintStrategy: When a first-action stem involves a client’s decision, choose the option that assesses understanding before options that document, persuade, or involve others.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client who is 2 days post hip repair has new-onset confusion, is picking at the air, and says, “Get me my shoes; I’m going home now.” She has a health care power of attorney naming her son and has never been declared incompetent by a court. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate regarding her request to leave?
options: Help her leave against medical advice because no court has found her incompetent
Ask the court to appoint a guardian before any further care decisions are made
Have her sign the against-medical-advice form because she is a legal adult
Treat this as a temporary loss of capacity and involve the provider and her son
optionRationales: Incorrect. This confuses legal competence with clinical capacity; she cannot make an informed choice while delirious.
Incorrect. Guardianship is for lasting incompetence; she already has an agent, and delirium may resolve.
Incorrect. A signature from a client who currently lacks capacity is not a valid informed refusal.
Correct. Acute confusion suggests delirium, which removes capacity for now; her agent and the provider are involved while the cause is treated.
questions.rationale: Competence is a legal status set by a court; capacity is the clinical ability, right now, to understand, weigh, and state a choice. Acute confusion after surgery suggests delirium, which can remove capacity temporarily even though she remains legally competent. Her durable power of attorney for health care takes effect when she lacks capacity, so the provider and her son are involved while the delirium is treated. Letting her leave because no court has ruled her incompetent is the most tempting error, because it treats a legal status as if it guaranteed clinical ability.
questions.takeaway: Competence is legal and lasting; capacity is clinical and can be lost temporarily from delirium, sedation, or intoxication.
questions.hintContent: Separate what a court has decided from what this client can do at this moment.
questions.hintStrategy: When options turn on look-alike terms, define each term and match it to the cues in the stem before choosing.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse at a community health center reviews actions taken by the nursing staff this week. Which actions best reflect the ethical principle of justice? Select all that apply.
options: Arranging a video sign language interpreter so a Deaf client can take part in her prenatal visit
Advocating that uninsured clients receive the same pain protocol as insured clients
Stopping a consent signing for a client who is drowsy after an opioid
Calling a client back at 1600 as promised with the results of her culture
Securing a transportation voucher so a rural client can keep his radiation appointments
Telling a client honestly that his biopsy result has not come back yet
optionRationales: Correct. An interpreter gives a Deaf client equal access to information and participation, which is fairness.
Correct. Equal treatment regardless of ability to pay is the core of justice.
Incorrect. Preventing harm to one client reflects nonmaleficence, not equal access.
Incorrect. Keeping a promise reflects fidelity, not justice.
Correct. Removing a distance barrier gives a rural client the same access to treatment as others.
Incorrect. Honest disclosure reflects veracity, not justice.
questions.rationale: Justice means fairness: arranging resources so every client has equal access to care regardless of disability, geography, or ability to pay. Interpreters, transportation, and equal pain protocols all remove barriers that would otherwise give some clients less care. Keeping a promised call is fidelity, and honest disclosure is veracity; both are ethical but are different principles. Stopping a drowsy client’s consent is the most tempting distractor because it is clearly good advocacy, but it protects one client from harm (nonmaleficence) rather than correcting unequal access.
questions.takeaway: Justice means fair, equal access; look for actions that remove a barrier tied to disability, distance, or money.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each action fixes an unfair difference in access or instead keeps a promise, tells the truth, or prevents harm.
questions.hintStrategy: For principle-sorting items, reduce the principle to one word (fairness) and test each option against only that word.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 71-year-old client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is brought to the emergency department by her husband with increasing shortness of breath. She is alert but can speak only one or two words at a time. The physician asks the nurse to set up for intubation, and the husband hands the nurse the document shown in the exhibit. What should the nurse do first?
options: Set up for intubation, then review the form with the physician afterward
Ask the husband whether he wants intubation now that she is in distress
Document the form in the chart and notify the charge nurse of the conflict
Show the physician the signed order declining intubation right away
optionRationales: Incorrect. Intubating first carries out the exact treatment she refused in writing.
Incorrect. The client is alert, and a family member does not override her signed order.
Incorrect. Documenting and escalating do not stop the physician who is about to intubate.
Correct. The physician must know the client’s documented refusal before the intervention she declined begins.

rows: Limited interventions: IV fluids, antibiotics, and oxygen by mask or cannula; do not intubate
Client and neurologist; dated 3 months ago

questions.rationale: Acting on behalf of the client means voicing her documented wishes to the team immediately, especially when she cannot speak easily. A signed portable medical order declining intubation must reach the physician before the procedure, because intubation is the exact intervention she refused. Treatments she did not refuse, such as oxygen, medications, and comfort care, continue, so honoring the order is not abandoning care. Intubating first and reviewing later is tempting under ABC logic, but airway priorities operate within the client’s legal, informed refusals.
questions.takeaway: When a treatment about to start conflicts with a written directive or portable medical order, tell the provider immediately; other wanted care continues.
questions.hintContent: Compare what the document allows with what it declines. Which one is about to happen?
questions.hintStrategy: ABC logic applies within the client’s documented wishes; when a stem includes a directive, check it before choosing an airway action.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 63-year-old client with COPD tells the clinic nurse, “I’m not getting the pneumonia shot. Vaccines just make you sick.” He is alert and has asked appropriate questions about his inhalers. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “If I were you, I’d get it, especially with your lungs.”
“What have you heard about vaccines making people sick?”
“That’s your choice, so I’ll just document that you declined.”
“Your provider ordered it, so I’ll go ahead and bring it in.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Offering a personal opinion pushes the nurse’s values and expresses disapproval.
Correct. Exploring his belief lets the nurse correct misinformation so his decision is informed, without approval or disapproval.
Incorrect. Respecting choice matters, but objectivity does not mean silence; this skips informing him.
Incorrect. Proceeding over a capable client’s refusal violates his autonomy.
questions.rationale: Safeguarding autonomy means a capable client makes the final choice, but only after receiving accurate information. Exploring his belief first lets the nurse address misinformation without showing approval or disapproval. Simply documenting the refusal is the tempting wrong answer because it seems respectful, yet objectivity does not mean silence, and an uninformed refusal is not fully autonomous. Offering a personal opinion or proceeding over his objection both override his right to decide.
questions.takeaway: Objective does not mean silent: explore beliefs and give facts, then respect the informed choice.
questions.hintContent: His refusal rests on a belief. What would make his choice truly informed?
questions.hintStrategy: In communication items, an open question that explores the client’s belief usually beats options that advise, comply, or close the topic.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A nurse manager audits nursing notes on an oncology unit. Which entries describe paternalism rather than advocacy and require follow-up with the nurses involved? Select all that apply.
options: “Held the client’s requested discharge papers until his daughter arrived to approve them.”
“Told the client that refusing a second chemotherapy cycle was unwise and asked her to reconsider.”
“Did not mention hospice as an option because the client seemed too fragile to hear it.”
“Asked the client privately whom she wants included in treatment discussions.”
“Notified the oncologist that the client wants to discuss stopping treatment.”
“Provided written radiation risks at a 6th-grade reading level at the client’s request.”
optionRationales: Correct. Requiring family approval for a capable adult’s request is paternalistic.
Correct. Expressing disapproval and pushing a capable client to change her mind overrides autonomy.
Correct. Withholding an option to protect the client decides for her and denies informed choice.
Incorrect. Letting the client decide who is involved respects her autonomy.
Incorrect. Communicating the client’s wish to the provider is advocacy.
Incorrect. Tailoring information to literacy safeguards autonomy.
questions.rationale: Paternalism is deciding for a client “for their own good” and overriding or bypassing an informed choice. Withholding hospice information, labeling a refusal unwise, and requiring family approval all substitute someone else’s judgment for a capable client’s. Advocacy instead gives clear information at the client’s literacy level, carries the client’s wishes to the provider, and lets the client choose who is involved. The hospice entry is the easiest to miss because it sounds compassionate, but protecting a client from information removes her ability to choose.
questions.takeaway: Advocacy supports the informed choice; paternalism overrides it, even when it sounds kind.
questions.hintContent: For each entry, ask who is making the decision: the client or someone acting for her good.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA items, judge each option independently against one test question rather than comparing options to each other.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 74-year-old Korean American client who speaks fluent English is admitted for weight loss, and a CT scan shows pancreatic cancer. Before the physician arrives to discuss the results, the client’s daughter tells the nurse, “Please don’t tell him it’s cancer. In our family, we protect our elders from bad news.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Agree to the request, because respecting the family’s culture is advocacy
Tell the daughter that the law requires the physician to disclose everything
Ask the client privately how much he wants to know and whom he wants involved
Ask the physician to delay the discussion until the family reaches agreement
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cultural respect does not allow family to override a capable client’s right to information.
Incorrect. This is confrontational and ignores that a capable client may choose not to know.
Correct. Only the capable client can say whether he wants full disclosure or prefers his family to receive information.
Incorrect. Family consensus is not required; delay withholds information from the client.
questions.rationale: In some collectivist cultures, families shield elders from serious news, and a capable client may freely choose to let family receive information; that choice is itself autonomy. The nurse cannot know which applies until the client is asked privately, without the family present. Agreeing with the daughter is the tempting wrong answer because it sounds culturally sensitive, but it lets the family override a capable client. Insisting on full disclosure is equally wrong if the client prefers not to know.
questions.takeaway: Never assume the family speaks for a capable client; ask the client privately how much he wants to know and who should decide.
questions.hintContent: Who has the right to decide how much this alert client hears about his own diagnosis?
questions.hintStrategy: When family and client interests may differ, choose the option that goes directly and privately to the capable client.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A clinic nurse noticed that clients with hourly jobs were missing daytime diabetes follow-up visits. She joined a hospital committee that added evening clinic hours 6 months ago. Which finding best indicates that this advocacy was effective?
options: Hospital leaders publicly thanked the nurse for her work on the committee
The committee voted to study adding weekend clinic hours sometime next year
One evening client said she likes the nurses who work in the evening clinic
Missed visits among clients with hourly jobs have dropped since then
optionRationales: Incorrect. Recognition of the nurse is not a client outcome.
Incorrect. A vote to study more changes describes process, not results.
Incorrect. One client’s satisfaction does not show change for the whole affected group.
Correct. A drop in missed visits in the target group shows the access barrier was actually reduced.
questions.rationale: Championing social justice is macrosocial advocacy aimed at removing a disparity, so success is measured by whether the gap narrowed for the affected group. A falling missed-visit rate among clients with hourly jobs shows the system barrier was reduced. Committee votes and praise describe process, not results. A single client’s satisfaction is tempting because it is positive feedback, but it does not show change for the population the nurse set out to help.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate system-level advocacy with a population outcome for the group that faced the barrier.
questions.hintContent: What was the original problem, and which option shows that problem got smaller?
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation items, match the outcome to the original problem; reject options that measure effort, process, or one person’s opinion.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse whose religious beliefs oppose organ donation is caring for a 45-year-old client recovering from a mild stroke. The client, who is alert and oriented, asks the nurse how to register as an organ donor. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Give accurate information on how to register or refer him to the resource
Explain that the nurse personally cannot discuss donation and change the subject
Suggest that he talk it over with his family first, since donation affects them
Ask the chaplain to visit so he can consider the moral questions involved
optionRationales: Correct. Professional ethics require accurate information without approval or disapproval, regardless of the nurse’s morals.
Incorrect. Refusing to engage abandons the client’s lawful request.
Incorrect. This subtly steers a capable adult and implies family approval is needed.
Incorrect. This frames a lawful choice as a moral problem and reflects the nurse’s beliefs.
questions.rationale: Morals are personal; professional ethics guide practice when the nurse’s morals conflict with a client’s legal, informed choice. The nurse must provide accurate information or connect the client with someone who can, without approval or disapproval. Sending the chaplain is tempting because it looks like a referral, but it treats a lawful choice as a moral problem and injects the nurse’s values. If the nurse cannot stay objective, she may ask a colleague to help, but she cannot simply refuse to engage.
questions.takeaway: When personal morals clash with a client’s lawful choice, give accurate information or hand off to a colleague; never impose your values.
questions.hintContent: Which guides the nurse at work: personal morals or the professional code?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that delay, redirect, or reframe the client’s request; choose the one that meets the request directly.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A nurse in a rural clinic completes an environmental exposure history, shown in the exhibit, for a 4-year-old with a speech delay and frequent abdominal pain. Which findings should the nurse identify as possible environmental hazards requiring follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Attendance at a preschool built in 2015
Drinking water from a municipal system with no advisories
An unvented kerosene heater with no carbon monoxide detector
Peeling paint in a home built before 1978
A parent who works with lead and brings work clothes home
optionRationales: Incorrect. A recently built preschool does not carry lead paint risk.
Incorrect. A regulated public system with no advisories is not a flagged hazard in this history.
Correct. Unvented combustion produces carbon monoxide, and there is no detector to warn the family.
Correct. Old paint is a major source of lead, which can cause developmental delay and abdominal pain.
Correct. Take-home dust from battery recycling is a known source of lead exposure for children.

rows: Rented farmhouse built in 1948; paint peeling on porch and windowsills
Father works at a battery recycling plant and changes clothes at home
Unvented kerosene space heater in the living room; no carbon monoxide detector
Attends a licensed preschool built in 2015

questions.rationale: An environmental exposure history looks at residence, present and past work, activities, and other concerns to find hazards that harm health. This child’s speech delay and abdominal pain fit lead exposure, and two findings point to it: pre-1978 peeling paint and a parent who brings lead dust home on work clothes. The unvented heater without a detector is a separate carbon monoxide risk that needs teaching and follow-up. The municipal water is the tempting distractor because water can carry lead, but a regulated system with no advisories is not the red flag in this history.
questions.takeaway: Old peeling paint, take-home work dust, and unvented fuel heaters are environmental red flags that call for screening and teaching.
questions.hintContent: Link the child’s symptoms to a known hazard, then look for any other exposure that could harm the household.
questions.hintStrategy: In exhibit-based SATA items, read each row and ask whether that specific detail creates a risk, rather than flagging every category.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A 32-year-old client is under general anesthesia for a laparoscopic appendectomy. Before surgery, she told the circulating nurse that she did not want students involved in her care. After induction, the attending surgeon says the two medical students can each do a pelvic exam “for practice, since she’s already asleep.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Allow the exams, because teaching is expected in an academic hospital
Tell the team she refused student involvement and never consented to an exam
Document the plan and report it to the nurse manager after the surgery
Ask the anesthesiologist to decide whether the exams may go ahead
optionRationales: Incorrect. Teaching never overrides a client’s refusal or lack of consent.
Correct. Voicing her stated wishes in real time protects an anesthetized client from a procedure she refused.
Incorrect. Reporting later does not protect the client from an exam happening now.
Incorrect. The anesthesiologist cannot consent for the client.
questions.rationale: When a client is anesthetized, the nurse acts on her behalf by voicing the wishes she stated while capable. An intimate exam she did not consent to, and that is unrelated to her procedure, violates her autonomy and must be stopped before it happens. Reporting after surgery is the tempting answer because escalation matters, but it does not protect her now. No one on the team can consent for her, and teaching never overrides a client’s refusal.
questions.takeaway: Under anesthesia, the nurse speaks up in real time for the wishes the client stated while awake.
questions.hintContent: The client cannot speak now. Who knows what she said before induction?
questions.hintStrategy: When harm is about to happen, choose the option that stops it now over options that report or defer.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 40-year-old client has been unresponsive on a ventilator for 3 weeks after a cardiac arrest, and the neurologist reports no meaningful chance of recovery. His wife, who is his health care agent, tells the nurse, “He always said he’d never want to live on machines, but I want everything done. I can’t lose him.” Which response by the nurse best supports the client?
options: “This is so hard. If he could speak now, what would he say he wants?”
“As his agent, you get to decide, so we will keep doing everything.”
“Continuing treatment is in his best interest until we are more certain.”
“The physician will decide what is medically best, so you don’t have to.”
optionRationales: Correct. This acknowledges her grief and refocuses the agent on the client’s own known wishes.
Incorrect. An agent’s role is to voice the client’s wishes, not her own preferences.
Incorrect. Best interest applies when wishes are unknown; his wishes are known.
Incorrect. This removes the lawful decision-maker and is paternalistic.
questions.rationale: Substituted judgment asks what the client would choose based on his known values, and it applies whenever those wishes are known. The health care agent’s job is to voice the client’s wishes, not her own, so the nurse gently refocuses her on what he said while acknowledging her grief. The best-interest standard is tempting because it sounds protective, but it is used only when the client’s wishes are unknown. Telling her the physician will decide removes the lawful decision-maker.
questions.takeaway: When wishes are known, use substituted judgment and ask what the client would choose; best interest is for unknown wishes.
questions.hintContent: The wife already told you what her husband said he wanted. Whose wishes should guide the agent?
questions.hintStrategy: For surrogate items, choose the response that keeps the focus on the client’s own values while acknowledging the family’s feelings.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: Over 6 months, a pediatric nurse notices that 11 children admitted for asthma exacerbations live in the same neighborhood beside a wood-processing plant, and parents report heavy dust on their cars each morning. Which nursing actions represent championing social justice? Select all that apply.
options: Writing a letter to the local newspaper about the neighborhood exposure
Referring one child with frequent attacks to a pediatric pulmonologist
Teaching each child’s parents correct spacer use with the inhaler
Reporting the cluster of cases to the local health department
Working with the state nurses association to support stronger air-quality rules
optionRationales: Correct. Public advocacy raises community awareness and pressure for change.
Incorrect. A referral for one child is microsocial and does not address the shared cause.
Incorrect. Individual teaching is valuable microsocial care but does not change the exposure.
Correct. Reporting a community pattern prompts investigation of a shared hazard, a macrosocial action.
Correct. Acting through a professional group to change policy is macrosocial advocacy.
questions.rationale: Championing social justice is macrosocial advocacy: working with organizations, communities, and policy to remove the cause of a disparity. A cluster of asthma cases near one plant signals a shared environmental hazard, so reporting to public health, supporting air-quality rules, and speaking publicly all target that cause. Inhaler teaching and specialist referral are tempting because they clearly help these children, but they work one client at a time and leave the exposure in place. Good advocates do both, yet only the system-level actions count as championing social justice.
questions.takeaway: When many clients share one cause, macrosocial advocacy targets the cause through public health, policy, and public voice.
questions.hintContent: Sort each action by level: does it help one child or change conditions for the whole neighborhood?
questions.hintStrategy: For micro versus macro items, label each option “one client” or “many clients/system” before selecting.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A 47-year-old client admitted for chest pain observation is alert, oriented, and pain-free with stable vital signs. His second troponin result is pending. He tells the nurse he is leaving to attend his daughter’s graduation in 2 hours, and his wife says, “Don’t let him go. Lock the doors if you have to.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the client what he understands about the risks of leaving at this time
Ask security to stand at the door until the provider can talk with him
Have the client sign the against-medical-advice form so he can leave on time
Tell the wife firmly that the decision belongs to the client, not to her
optionRationales: Correct. Assessing his understanding and reasons is the first step toward an informed decision and possible alternatives.
Incorrect. Detaining a capable adult overrides his autonomy and may be false imprisonment.
Incorrect. Signing the form skips confirming that his decision is informed.
Incorrect. This is accurate but blunt, and it skips assessing the client’s understanding.
questions.rationale: A capable adult may leave against advice, but the choice should be informed. The first step is to assess what he understands about the risks and why he wants to leave, which also helps the team look for alternatives, such as expediting the troponin result, and prepares the provider to explain the risks. Detaining him would override a capable client. Telling the wife the choice is his is accurate, which makes it tempting, but it skips the assessment that makes his decision informed.
questions.takeaway: When a capable client wants to leave, assess understanding and reasons first; never detain or coerce.
questions.hintContent: He is alert and stable. What do you need to know before his choice can be called informed?
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act: when no emergency exists, the first step is usually gathering the client’s understanding.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: During an admission interview, a 56-year-old client who recently moved from rural India says, with her husband sitting beside her, “My husband decides about my health. Please talk to him.” Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Explain that U.S. law requires adult clients to make their own decisions
Direct all further questions and teaching to her husband from now on
Ask the husband to wait outside whenever any decision has to be made
Confirm this preference with the client privately and document her choice
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is inaccurate; a capable client may choose to let family decide.
Incorrect. This assumes the choice is voluntary without verifying it with her alone.
Incorrect. This overrides the preference she just expressed.
Correct. A capable client may hand off decisions; confirming privately verifies the choice is truly hers.
questions.rationale: A capable client who freely chooses to let a family member decide is exercising autonomy, and collectivist cultures often express decision-making this way. Because her husband was present, the nurse confirms privately, with a qualified interpreter if needed, that the choice is truly hers, and then documents it. Routing everything to the husband is tempting because it honors the stated wish, but it skips verifying that the wish is voluntary. Insisting she decide alone imposes a Western view of autonomy.
questions.takeaway: A client who freely hands decisions to family is using autonomy; confirm it privately and document it.
questions.hintContent: Was her statement made freely? How could the nurse find out?
questions.hintStrategy: In cultural items, choose the option that respects the client’s stated preference and verifies it directly with her.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: Through a qualified interpreter, a 52-year-old Vietnamese client with limited English proficiency is told that her clinical breast exam found a lump and that a mammogram is recommended. She replies, “It does not hurt, so it is nothing. I do not need that test.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Explain that painless lumps can be cancer and book the mammogram today
Document that she declined the mammogram and notify the provider
Ask her adult daughter in the waiting room to encourage her to have it
Ask, through the interpreter, what she believes a painless lump means
optionRationales: Incorrect. Teaching before exploring her belief is less effective, and booking the test overrides her choice.
Incorrect. Her refusal is based on a belief that has not been explored, so it is not yet informed.
Incorrect. Recruiting family bypasses the client and pressures her.
Correct. Exploring her belief first allows culturally tailored teaching that addresses it.
questions.rationale: In traditional Vietnamese culture, some believe a breast lump matters only if it hurts or grows, which can delay diagnosis. The nurse first explores the client’s belief so that teaching can address it respectfully and in culturally tailored language. Explaining that painless lumps can be cancer is the tempting answer because it is accurate, but teaching before understanding her belief is less effective, and booking the test overrides her choice. After exploring and teaching, the nurse respects her final informed decision.
questions.takeaway: With a culturally based refusal, explore the belief first, then teach in tailored language and respect the final choice.
questions.hintContent: Her statement reveals a belief. What should happen before any teaching?
questions.hintStrategy: When a client’s reasoning is unclear, choose the option that explores it before options that teach, document, or recruit others.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A nurse helped a 69-year-old client with low health literacy and newly diagnosed colon cancer write down her goals and questions before her oncology visit. Which observation during the visit best indicates the nurse’s advocacy was effective?
options: She quickly agrees to whichever treatment plan the oncologist recommends first
She tells the oncologist her goal and asks how each option affects it
She says, “Whatever you think is best, doctor; you know more than I do.”
Her son reads her written questions aloud and then answers them for her
optionRationales: Incorrect. Agreement alone does not show understanding or participation.
Correct. Stating her own goal and asking how options fit it shows active participation in the decision.
Incorrect. Deferring entirely to the physician shows she is not taking part.
Incorrect. Family answering for her shows the client is not participating.
questions.rationale: Safeguarding autonomy aims for a client who shares her own goals and values and takes part in decisions at her literacy level. A client who states her goal and asks how options affect it is actively participating, which is the outcome the nurse worked toward. Quick agreement with the first recommendation is tempting because it looks like cooperation, but agreement alone does not show the client understood or shaped the decision. Deferring entirely to the physician or a family member shows the goal was not met.
questions.takeaway: Effective autonomy advocacy shows up as a client who voices her own goals and asks questions, not one who simply agrees.
questions.hintContent: The nurse prepared her to share goals and ask questions. Which option shows her doing both?
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation items, choose the option that demonstrates the behavior the intervention was designed to produce.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: Over 2 days, an emergency department nurse cares for three households with headache, dizziness, and nausea. All clients are now receiving oxygen and are stable. The nurse reviews the information shown in the exhibit. Which action should the nurse take next to address the underlying problem?
options: Teach each household to buy a carbon monoxide detector before going home
Document the address in each client’s chart for follow-up at the next visit
Report the cluster to the local health department for investigation
Refer each household to a primary care provider for follow-up evaluation
optionRationales: Incorrect. Individual teaching helps but leaves the source in place and neighbors exposed.
Incorrect. Documentation alone does nothing to stop ongoing exposure.
Correct. Other residents are still exposed; reporting the pattern targets the shared source.
Incorrect. Follow-up care does not address the source still exposing other residents.

rows: Headache and nausea; began after the building heat was turned on
Headache and fatigue; says neighbors feel the same

questions.rationale: Several households from one building with the same symptoms after the heat was turned on is a pattern pointing to a shared carbon monoxide source. Once each client is stable, the next step is reporting the cluster so public health and building authorities can investigate, because other residents are still being exposed. Teaching each family to buy a detector is tempting because it is good individual teaching, but it leaves the source in place and does not protect neighbors. Environmental hazards that cluster in one place call for macrosocial action.
questions.takeaway: The same exposure illness in several people from one place calls for reporting to public health, not only individual teaching.
questions.hintContent: Look at the address column. What does the pattern tell you about who else is at risk?
questions.hintStrategy: When an exhibit shows a pattern across clients, the best answer usually addresses the shared cause rather than each client separately.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A 6-year-old is 8 hours post-appendectomy. He is lying very still, grimacing, and crying quietly. His father says, “He’s just being dramatic; he doesn’t need any more medicine.” The last PRN analgesic dose was 5 hours ago. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give the PRN analgesic now, because the child is clearly in pain
Assess the child’s pain using an age-appropriate faces rating scale
Explain to the father that grimacing and crying are signs of pain
Notify the surgeon that the current pain plan is not working
optionRationales: Incorrect. Strong cues suggest pain, but a rating is needed first to choose the dose and evaluate it.
Correct. A validated rating gives data to choose the right dose, inform the father, and evaluate the response.
Incorrect. Teaching the father is useful after the nurse has assessment data to share.
Incorrect. There is no assessment yet to show the plan has failed.
questions.rationale: Acting on behalf of a child includes making sure his pain is recognized and treated even when a parent minimizes it. Assessment comes first: a faces scale validated for his age provides data to select the correct PRN dose and to share with the father and provider. Giving the analgesic immediately is tempting because the cues strongly suggest pain, but the nurse needs a rating to choose the dose and evaluate the response. Teaching the father and notifying the surgeon both depend on what the assessment shows.
questions.takeaway: Advocating for a child’s comfort starts with an age-appropriate assessment, then action.
questions.hintContent: No emergency is present. Which step of the nursing process comes before giving the medication?
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act unless the situation is an emergency; look for an assessment option tailored to the client’s age.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with heart failure is alert and has told the nurse twice that he does not want an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator because he “doesn’t want to be shocked at the end.” On rounds, the cardiologist schedules the implant for tomorrow and says, “He’ll come around once I explain it again.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Tell the cardiologist that the client has clearly refused the device
Begin preprocedure teaching so the client knows what to expect tomorrow
Have the client sign a refusal form and place it on the front of the chart
Ask the ethics committee to review the disagreement before tomorrow
optionRationales: Correct. Speaking up directly to the provider is the first step when a plan ignores a capable client’s stated wishes.
Incorrect. Preprocedure teaching assumes a consent the client has not given.
Incorrect. A form without a discussion bypasses the provider who needs to hear the refusal.
Incorrect. Escalation may follow, but the nurse first communicates directly with the provider.
questions.rationale: Advocacy includes speaking up when a provider moves forward against a competent client’s stated wishes. The quickest, most direct step is telling the cardiologist about the client’s clear refusal so the plan can be revisited with the client. Requesting an ethics consult is tempting because it involves the team, but escalation comes after the nurse first communicates with the provider. Preprocedure teaching assumes consent he has not given, and a refusal form without discussion bypasses the provider.
questions.takeaway: When a provider’s plan ignores a capable client’s stated wishes, speak up to that provider first, then escalate if needed.
questions.hintContent: Who needs to hear the client’s words before tomorrow?
questions.hintStrategy: Follow the chain: communicate directly with the person involved before going to committees or higher levels.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse at a rural health center in eastern North Carolina treats four migrant farmworkers in one week for heat exhaustion. All work on the same farm and say water and shade breaks are rarely allowed. After each client is treated and stable, which action best demonstrates championing social justice?
options: Teaching each worker the early signs of heat illness and how to rehydrate
Reporting the farm’s conditions to occupational safety officials
Documenting each worker’s occupation and symptoms in the health record
Giving each worker a refillable water bottle before discharge from the clinic
optionRationales: Incorrect. Teaching is useful microsocial care but does not change the working conditions.
Correct. Reporting an unsafe workplace to the responsible agency targets the cause for all workers.
Incorrect. Documentation supports care but does not change conditions on the farm.
Incorrect. A water bottle helps one worker but does not ensure breaks or shade.
questions.rationale: Championing social justice means acting at the organizational, community, or policy level to remove the cause of harm to a group. Four workers from one farm with the same heat illness point to an unsafe workplace, so reporting the conditions to occupational safety officials, ideally alongside worker advocacy groups, addresses the cause for everyone there. Teaching heat-illness signs is tempting because it is good nursing care, but it places the burden on workers who report they are not allowed breaks. Workplace exposures and extreme heat are environmental hazards that fall hardest on low-income workers.
questions.takeaway: A pattern of workplace illness calls for reporting and system change, not only individual teaching.
questions.hintContent: The workers already know they need water and shade. What is actually stopping them?
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem describes the same harm in several clients from one source, look for the option that reaches the source.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 29-year-old client is brought to the emergency department after falling while intoxicated. He has a scalp laceration, slurred speech, and a strong odor of alcohol, and he cannot remember the fall. He stands up, pulls off his cardiac leads, and says, “I’m out of here.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Have the client sign the against-medical-advice form before he leaves
Let the client leave, because he is an adult with a right to refuse care
Stay with the client, keep him safe, and call the provider to see him now
Ask security to place the client in four-point restraints right away
optionRationales: Incorrect. A client whose capacity is impaired cannot give an informed refusal.
Incorrect. The right to refuse depends on capacity, which intoxication and head injury may remove.
Correct. His capacity is in doubt, so the nurse protects his safety and gets an immediate provider evaluation.
Incorrect. Restraints are not the first or least restrictive step.
questions.rationale: Intoxication and a possible head injury can remove decision-making capacity temporarily, so this client may not be able to make an informed refusal right now. Acting on his behalf means keeping him safe and getting the provider to evaluate his capacity and injury immediately. Letting him leave is tempting because adults can refuse care, but that right depends on capacity, which his memory loss, slurred speech, and intoxication call into question. Four-point restraints are not the first or least restrictive step.
questions.takeaway: A client whose capacity is impaired by intoxication or injury cannot give an informed refusal; protect safety and get a capacity evaluation.
questions.hintContent: Can this client understand and weigh the risks of leaving right now?
questions.hintStrategy: When capacity is uncertain and safety is at risk, choose the least restrictive option that keeps the client safe and brings in the provider.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: During a colonoscopy under moderate sedation, a 61-year-old client becomes restless and says repeatedly, “Stop, stop, it hurts. I want you to stop.” The gastroenterologist keeps advancing the scope and says, “We’re almost done.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Tell the gastroenterologist the client is asking to stop and is in pain
Give the next PRN sedation dose as ordered to help the client relax
Hold the client’s hand and reassure him that the procedure is almost over
Document the client’s statements and pain rating in the procedure record
optionRationales: Correct. Voicing the client’s words lets the physician pause and respond to his request and pain.
Incorrect. Sedating him before raising his request silences his objection.
Incorrect. Reassurance does not address a client asking for the procedure to stop.
Incorrect. Documentation does not stop a procedure the client is asking to end.
questions.rationale: A sedated client keeps the right to withdraw consent and to have pain addressed, and the nurse acts on his behalf by voicing his words to the physician right away. The physician must then pause and decide with the client whether to stop, adjust sedation, or explain and obtain agreement. Giving more sedation is tempting because it treats discomfort, but doing so before raising his request silences his objection. Reassurance and documentation do not stop a procedure the client is asking to end.
questions.takeaway: When a sedated client says stop, voice it to the provider immediately; the client’s words, not the schedule, guide the procedure.
questions.hintContent: The client cannot advocate for himself well right now. Who must hear what he is saying?
questions.hintStrategy: When the client is objecting during a procedure, choose communication with the provider over comfort or documentation options.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 44-year-old client with schizophrenia who is not under guardianship is calm and explains that a colonoscopy could find cancer early, but he does not want one because he had a bad reaction to sedation before. A staff member says, “He’s psych; his family should decide.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “You’re right; we should call his family so they can sign for the procedure.”
“We should ask a court to declare him incompetent before he refuses.”
“Capacity depends on what he can understand and weigh, not his diagnosis.”
“He can refuse now, but his psychiatrist must approve the refusal.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A psychiatric diagnosis does not transfer decisions to family.
Incorrect. Seeking a court ruling assumes incapacity he does not show.
Correct. Capacity depends on understanding, weighing, and stating a choice, which he demonstrates.
Incorrect. No one must approve a capable client’s refusal.
questions.rationale: Capacity is the clinical ability to understand information, weigh options, and state a choice, and this client explains the benefit and his reason for declining. A psychiatric diagnosis alone does not remove capacity or legal competence, and he has no guardian. Seeking a court ruling is tempting for a cautious nurse, but it assumes incapacity that he does not show and delays respecting his choice. His decision is documented and shared with the provider, who may explore sedation alternatives with him.
questions.takeaway: A diagnosis never decides capacity; the client’s ability to understand, weigh, and choose does.
questions.hintContent: List what the client is able to do in this stem, then compare it with what capacity requires.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject options that make a decision based on a label; choose the one based on the client’s demonstrated abilities.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A nurse in a rural Appalachian clinic wants to increase colorectal cancer screening. Many clients say, “If it’s meant to be, it’ll happen,” and the nearest endoscopy center is 70 miles away. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Telling clients that fatalistic beliefs are not supported by science
Teaching about screening in plain language with locally relevant examples
Asking clients, “Tell me more about what you believe about cancer”
Offering a mail-in stool test when it fits the client’s screening plan
Scheduling colonoscopies for all eligible clients without asking first
Limiting teaching to clients who already say they want screening
optionRationales: Incorrect. Dismissing beliefs damages trust and does not change behavior.
Correct. Plain, culturally tailored teaching improves understanding.
Correct. Exploring beliefs first allows respectful, targeted teaching.
Correct. A home test lowers the travel barrier for eligible clients.
Incorrect. Scheduling without consent overrides client choice.
Incorrect. This leaves the most at-risk clients without information.
questions.rationale: In Appalachia, fatalistic beliefs, low income, and access barriers lower screening rates. Effective advocacy explores beliefs first, teaches in plain, culturally tailored language, and lowers travel and cost barriers, such as offering a home stool test when appropriate. Telling clients their beliefs are unscientific is tempting because it seems to correct misinformation, but it dismisses their culture and closes the conversation. Scheduling without asking overrides choice, and limiting teaching to interested clients misses those who most need it.
questions.takeaway: For culturally shaped health behavior: explore beliefs, teach in tailored language, and remove access barriers.
questions.hintContent: Two problems appear in the stem: a belief and a distance. Which options address each respectfully?
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA items about culture, select options that explore, tailor, or remove barriers; reject options that dismiss or decide for clients.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A perioperative nurse is caring for a client who will be under general anesthesia for a hysterectomy. Which actions show the nurse acting on behalf of the client during this time? Select all that apply.
options: Monitoring her positioning and padding to protect her from pressure injury
Deciding, based on the nurse’s judgment, whether to remove an unexpected ovarian cyst
Asking her sister in the waiting room to approve a change in her code status
Confirming before induction that the team knows her advance directive and code status
Speaking up if the team proposes a procedure that she did not consent to
optionRationales: Correct. Monitoring safety and quality of care for a client who cannot protect herself is acting on behalf.
Incorrect. The nurse does not become the decision-maker; this is outside the nurse’s role.
Incorrect. A capable client’s documented wishes stand; a relative cannot change them during surgery.
Correct. Sharing her documented wishes before she loses the ability to speak protects them.
Correct. Voicing her lack of consent protects her autonomy while she is anesthetized.
questions.rationale: Acting on behalf of the client applies when she cannot speak for herself, as during anesthesia. The nurse shares her documented wishes with the team, monitors care for safety, and speaks up if treatment goes against her consent or wishes. The nurse does not become the decision-maker, so judging whether to remove an unexpected finding is the tempting wrong answer; it looks protective, but it substitutes the nurse’s preferences. A relative cannot alter the code status a capable client set before surgery.
questions.takeaway: Acting on behalf means voicing known wishes, monitoring safety, and speaking up, never substituting your own decisions.
questions.hintContent: Is each action protecting her known wishes and safety, or making a new decision for her?
questions.hintStrategy: For role-based SATA items, reject options in which the nurse takes over a decision that belongs to the client or surrogate.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A capable 77-year-old client with end-stage kidney disease has decided, after discussion with the nephrologist, to stop dialysis and begin hospice care. Which statements by the nurse maintain objectivity while supporting the client? Select all that apply.
options: “You’re so brave; I think you made the right decision.”
“If you have more questions about symptoms, I can ask the nephrologist to come back.”
“I’ll make sure the hospice team has your wishes in writing.”
“Have you thought about how your grandchildren will feel?”
“What questions do you still have about what to expect?”
“Most clients in your situation keep going with dialysis.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Expressing approval is not objective; it injects the nurse’s opinion.
Correct. Connecting the client with the provider supports the discussion objectively.
Correct. Communicating the client’s wishes supports her decision without approval or disapproval.
Incorrect. Invoking family feelings induces guilt and pressures the client.
Correct. An open question supports informed choice without judgment.
Incorrect. This is pressure that implies disapproval.
questions.rationale: Objectivity means staying involved and giving facts while showing neither approval nor disapproval of a capable client’s informed decision. Open questions, connecting the client with the provider, and communicating her wishes to the next team all support her without judgment. Praising her choice is the most tempting wrong answer because it feels supportive, but approval is the same error as disapproval in the opposite direction. Comparing her with other clients or invoking family feelings pressures her to change her mind.
questions.takeaway: Objective support gives facts and connects resources without approving, disapproving, or pressuring.
questions.hintContent: Check each statement for any hint of the nurse’s own opinion about the decision.
questions.hintStrategy: In communication SATA items, eliminate statements that judge, compare, or induce guilt, even if they sound warm.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A charge nurse is making rounds on a medical unit. Which situations require the nurse to intervene as the clients’ advocate? Select all that apply.
options: A technician tells a client, “No pain medicine until you agree to the scan”
A son asks staff not to tell his alert mother her biopsy results
A tube feeding is about to start for a client whose living will refuses it
An alert client declines one physical therapy session after discussing the benefits
A capable client has chosen to let her eldest daughter make her decisions
A client with dementia and his health care agent both agree on comfort-focused care
optionRationales: Correct. Using threats to obtain agreement is coercion and violates voluntary consent.
Correct. Family may not hide information from a capable client without her choice.
Correct. A treatment about to begin against a written directive must be stopped and raised with the provider.
Incorrect. This is an informed choice by a capable client, which the nurse respects.
Incorrect. Freely handing off decisions is an exercise of autonomy.
Incorrect. The legal decision-maker and the client’s wishes align; no conflict exists.
questions.rationale: Advocacy red flags include family trying to hide information from or override a capable client, pressure or threats used to gain agreement, and a treatment about to start against a written directive. Each of these violates autonomy or acts against known wishes and requires the nurse to intervene. A capable client declining one session after discussion, or choosing to let a relative decide, is autonomy in action rather than a problem. The delegated-decision situation is the most tempting to select, but a free choice to let family decide is itself respected.
questions.takeaway: Intervene when someone overrides, pressures, or acts against a client’s known wishes; respect informed choices, including the choice to let family decide.
questions.hintContent: In each situation, ask whether the client’s own informed wishes are being respected or overridden.
questions.hintStrategy: For red-flag SATA items, select only situations where something is wrong now, not situations that merely look unusual.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is assisting the provider in determining whether a 79-year-old client with mild cognitive impairment has the capacity to decide about a pacemaker. Which findings support that the client currently has decision-making capacity? Select all that apply.
options: She states the same choice clearly in two separate conversations
She agrees with the cardiologist’s recommendation without asking questions
Her daughter tells the nurse that her mother understands everything
She explains in her own words what a pacemaker does and its main risks
She compares having the device with not having it in terms of her own goals
optionRationales: Correct. Clearly communicating a consistent choice is part of capacity.
Incorrect. Agreement alone does not show understanding or reasoning.
Incorrect. Capacity is shown by the client, not reported by family.
Correct. Understanding the information is a core element of capacity.
Correct. Weighing options against personal values shows reasoning.
questions.rationale: Capacity is a clinical judgment, made by the provider with nursing input, about whether the client can understand information, weigh options, and state a choice right now. A diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment does not by itself remove capacity, and this client demonstrates all three abilities. Agreement with the physician is the tempting distractor because it seems cooperative, but agreeing without questions shows neither understanding nor reasoning. A family member’s report is not evidence of what the client can do.
questions.takeaway: Capacity is shown by the client understanding, weighing, and stating a choice, not by agreeing or by family report.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three abilities that make up capacity and look for the client demonstrating each.
questions.hintStrategy: For assessment SATA items, select findings the client demonstrates directly; be wary of secondhand reports and simple agreement.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 57-year-old client is scheduled for a thyroidectomy in 2 hours. As the nurse prepares to witness the consent signature, the client says, “I’m not really sure if they’re taking all of it or part of it, but the surgeon is so busy that I didn’t want to bother her.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Hold off on witnessing and tell the surgeon the client needs more explanation
Explain the difference between a total and a partial thyroidectomy to the client
Witness the signature, since the client is alert and willing to proceed
Notify the operating room that the surgery must be canceled today
optionRationales: Correct. The client cannot state the procedure, so consent is not informed; the surgeon must explain it.
Incorrect. Explaining the procedure for consent is the surgeon’s responsibility, and the nurse may misstate the plan.
Incorrect. Willingness without understanding is not informed consent.
Incorrect. There is time for the surgeon to clarify; canceling is premature and not the nurse’s decision.
questions.rationale: Valid consent requires capacity, information, and free choice, and this client cannot state what procedure she is agreeing to. The nurse does not witness the signature and notifies the surgeon, who must explain the procedure and answer her questions. Explaining the surgery herself is the tempting wrong answer, but providing the information for consent is the surgeon’s responsibility, and the nurse could misstate the planned extent. Canceling is premature because there is time for the surgeon to clarify before surgery.
questions.takeaway: If a client cannot explain the procedure, do not witness; notify the provider, who must explain it.
questions.hintContent: Which of the three parts of valid consent is missing here, and whose job is it to supply it?
questions.hintStrategy: In consent items, the nurse verifies and reports; eliminate options in which the nurse explains, decides, or proceeds anyway.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 54-year-old client who speaks only Spanish has signed consent for a colonoscopy with possible polyp removal. His 15-year-old daughter interpreted the discussion and now tells the nurse, “I didn’t know how to say ‘perforation,’ so I told him it was safe.” He has not received any sedation. What should the nurse do first?
options: Tell the physician that a major risk was never interpreted for him
Ask the daughter to look up the Spanish word and explain the risk to him now
Have a qualified interpreter explain perforation to him and then witness again
Proceed, because the client signed the form and has not been sedated
optionRationales: Correct. The physician must repeat the discussion through a qualified interpreter before the procedure.
Incorrect. A minor should not interpret consent, and the risk must come from the physician.
Incorrect. An interpreter conveys the physician’s words; the physician must give the explanation.
Incorrect. A signature obtained without a major risk being explained is not informed consent.
questions.rationale: Consent is invalid when a major risk was never conveyed, and a minor should not interpret consent discussions because of errors and the burden placed on the child. The first step is to notify the physician, who must repeat the discussion through a qualified medical interpreter and obtain a new signature if the client agrees. Having an interpreter explain the risk is tempting because it fixes the language barrier, but the risks must be explained by the physician, with the interpreter conveying the physician’s words. Proceeding on the existing signature violates the client’s autonomy.
questions.takeaway: A signature does not make consent valid; if a key risk was missed, the provider repeats the discussion through a qualified interpreter.
questions.hintContent: Was the client informed? Who is responsible for informing him?
questions.hintStrategy: When consent is flawed, the first action is almost always notifying the provider; options that let others fix it skip the responsible person.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client is scheduled for an elective total knee replacement. When the nurse brings the unsigned consent form, the client says quietly, “My son already took time off work to be here. He wants me to have this, but I really don’t want surgery.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Notify the surgeon that the client has canceled the knee replacement
Ask the client to tell the nurse more about what she wants for her knee
Witness the signature, because she is capable and the surgery is elective
Remind the client that she can change her mind after signing the form
optionRationales: Incorrect. She has not canceled; the nurse needs to understand her wishes first.
Correct. Exploring her own wishes clarifies whether her choice would be voluntary before anything is signed.
Incorrect. Capacity is only one element; free choice appears to be missing.
Incorrect. This still lets a pressured signature stand.
questions.rationale: Consent must be voluntary, and this client’s statement signals family pressure and a personal wish not to have surgery. The first action is to explore her own wishes; if she does not want the surgery, the nurse does not witness and tells the surgeon. Witnessing because she is capable is the most tempting wrong answer, but capacity is only one of the three elements, and free choice is in doubt. Reminding her she can withdraw later still lets a pressured signature stand.
questions.takeaway: Consent requires capacity, information, and free choice; when pressure appears, explore the client’s own wishes before anything is signed.
questions.hintContent: Whose wish is driving this surgery?
questions.hintStrategy: When a client expresses doubt or pressure, choose the open, exploring option before options that act on assumptions.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A home health nurse has visited an 84-year-old widower with early Parkinson disease weekly for a year. He has no children and says, “You know me better than anyone. I want you to be the one who makes my medical decisions if I can’t.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “I’d be honored. I’ll make sure all of your wishes are followed if you can’t speak.”
“I can’t be your decision-maker as your nurse, but I can help you pick someone.”
“If you can’t decide for yourself, I’ll choose what I think is best for you.”
“You don’t need to name anyone, because the state will choose for you.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The client’s own nurse serving as surrogate is a conflict of interest.
Correct. This declines a conflict of interest while helping him name a surrogate and document his wishes.
Incorrect. This accepts the role and applies the nurse’s preferences rather than his wishes.
Incorrect. This discourages planning and leaves his wishes undocumented.
questions.rationale: The nurse caring for a client may not act as that client’s surrogate, because it creates a conflict of interest with serious legal consequences. The nurse can still advocate by helping him consider whom he trusts and connecting him with a social worker or attorney to complete a durable power of attorney for health care and a living will. Accepting the role is tempting because it honors the relationship, but it compromises objectivity and professional boundaries. Telling him no planning is needed leaves his wishes undocumented.
questions.takeaway: The client’s own nurse is never the client’s surrogate; help the client name someone else and document wishes.
questions.hintContent: What conflict arises if the person giving care also makes the care decisions?
questions.hintStrategy: For boundary-related requests, choose the response that declines the role kindly and redirects to a helpful alternative.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: An adult client is brought to the emergency department unresponsive after a motorcycle crash. His blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg, and a CT scan shows a ruptured spleen. He has no identification, and staff cannot reach any family. The surgeon wants to operate immediately. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Prepare the client for surgery under emergency implied consent
Wait for hospital legal counsel to approve the surgery before transport
Have two nurses sign the consent form on the client’s behalf
Ask the bystander who called 911 to sign as the client’s representative
optionRationales: Correct. A life-threatening emergency with no capable client or reachable surrogate allows treatment under implied consent.
Incorrect. Waiting delays life-saving care the law already permits.
Incorrect. Nurses have no authority to consent for a client.
Incorrect. A bystander is not a legal surrogate.
questions.rationale: In a true emergency, when a client cannot consent and no surrogate can be reached, implied consent allows life-saving treatment because a reasonable person would agree to it. This client is hypotensive with a ruptured spleen, so delay threatens his life. Waiting for legal counsel is tempting because it seems cautious, but it delays care that is already permitted. Nurses and bystanders have no authority to sign as surrogates; the team documents the emergency and the efforts to reach family.
questions.takeaway: In a life-threatening emergency with no capable client or surrogate, treat under implied consent and document efforts to reach family.
questions.hintContent: Is this an emergency, and is anyone available who can legally consent?
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem shows instability and no surrogate, choose the option that treats now; reject options that delay or use people without authority.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 45-year-old client in the preoperative holding area signed consent yesterday for a laparoscopic hysterectomy. While the nurse is starting her IV, the client says, “I’ve changed my mind. I don’t want to go through with this today.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Remind the client that she already signed the consent form yesterday
Give the prescribed preoperative anxiolytic to help her feel calmer
Ask her partner to talk with her about why the surgery is needed
Stop the preoperative preparations and notify the surgeon
optionRationales: Incorrect. A signed form does not obligate her to proceed.
Incorrect. Sedating a client who is withdrawing consent undermines her ability to decide.
Incorrect. Recruiting family to persuade her pressures a capable client.
Correct. Consent can be withdrawn at any time, so preparation stops and the surgeon is informed.
questions.rationale: A client may withdraw consent at any time, even after signing, and a signed form does not obligate her to proceed. The nurse stops preparations and notifies the surgeon, who can discuss her concerns and confirm her decision. Giving the anxiolytic is the tempting wrong answer because anxiety is common before surgery, but sedating a client who is withdrawing consent undermines her ability to decide. Involving her partner to persuade her pressures a capable client.
questions.takeaway: Consent can be withdrawn at any time; stop and notify the provider rather than persuade or sedate.
questions.hintContent: Does a signature from yesterday bind her today?
questions.hintStrategy: When a client withdraws consent, choose the option that stops and reports; reject options that persuade, remind, or medicate.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 38-year-old client with bipolar disorder tells the community mental health nurse that staff at his former group home hit him and kept his monthly check. He wants an agency that can investigate and protect his rights. Which resource best fits this request?
options: The local affiliate of the National Alliance on Mental Illness
A peer support group that meets weekly at the community center
The state protection and advocacy agency for people with mental illness
The regional office that handles Americans with Disabilities Act claims
optionRationales: Incorrect. NAMI offers support, education, and advocacy, not abuse investigations.
Incorrect. Peer support may help him cope but cannot investigate abuse.
Correct. These federally mandated agencies investigate abuse and neglect and protect rights.
Incorrect. ADA enforcement addresses disability discrimination, not abuse in a group home.
questions.rationale: Protection and Advocacy for Individuals with Mental Illness (PAIMI) agencies are federally mandated state agencies that investigate abuse and neglect and protect the rights of people with mental illness; in North Carolina this is Disability Rights North Carolina. NAMI is the tempting look-alike because it is well known in mental health, but it provides support, education, and advocacy rather than investigation. The ADA addresses discrimination in jobs, schools, transportation, and public places. The nurse also reports the allegation through required channels and confirms the client is currently safe.
questions.takeaway: PAIMI agencies investigate abuse and protect rights; NAMI supports and educates.
questions.hintContent: The client asked for investigation and protection. Which agency’s job is that?
questions.hintStrategy: For resource-matching items, match the client’s specific request to each agency’s core function.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A 41-year-old client who is Deaf and communicates in American Sign Language (ASL) needs consent for a cardiac catheterization. The cardiologist begins writing notes back and forth, and the client’s hearing 13-year-old son offers to sign for his mother. What should the nurse do first?
options: Accept the son’s offer, because he signs with his mother every day
Continue with written notes, because the client can read and write English
Ask the client to nod after each sentence to show that she understands
Request a qualified ASL interpreter to be present in person or by video
optionRationales: Incorrect. A child should not interpret consent because of errors and the burden on him.
Incorrect. For many ASL users, English is a second language, and notes often omit risks and limit questions.
Incorrect. Nodding does not demonstrate understanding.
Correct. A qualified interpreter gives her complete information and lets her ask questions in her own language.
questions.rationale: A client who is Deaf is entitled to a qualified interpreter under the Americans with Disabilities Act, so she receives complete information and can ask questions in her own language. A child should not interpret consent because of errors, omissions, and the burden it places on him. Written notes are tempting because the client reads English, but for many ASL users English is a second language, and notes often leave out risks and discourage questions. Nodding does not show understanding.
questions.takeaway: For consent, use a qualified medical interpreter, including ASL, never a family member or child.
questions.hintContent: Which option gives this client the same access to information that a hearing client would have?
questions.hintStrategy: In interpreter items, choose the qualified professional option; eliminate family, children, and shortcuts.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 26-year-old client with a moderate intellectual disability has a court-appointed guardian, his aunt, who has signed consent for a dental extraction under sedation. In the preprocedure area, the client pulls away, covers his mouth, and says, “No hurt. Go home.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Proceed with the procedure, because the guardian has given valid consent
Request an order for restraints so the procedure can be done safely
Ask the client in simple words what is worrying him about the procedure
Cancel the procedure, because the client has refused treatment
optionRationales: Incorrect. Valid consent does not remove the nurse’s duty to involve the client at his level.
Incorrect. Restraint is not a first response to fear.
Correct. Exploring his fear lets the nurse address it and share it with the guardian and provider.
Incorrect. The guardian holds decision-making authority; canceling outright bypasses her.
questions.rationale: When a guardian holds legal decision-making authority, the guardian consents, but the nurse still explains the procedure in simple terms, seeks the client’s agreement, and conveys his fears to the guardian and provider. Asking what worries him may reveal a fear, such as pain, that can be addressed with explanation or comfort measures. Proceeding because consent is signed is tempting, but it ignores his distress and his right to be heard. Canceling outright overrides the guardian’s authority, and restraint is not a first response to fear.
questions.takeaway: Even when a guardian consents, involve the client at his level and share his fears with the guardian and provider.
questions.hintContent: The paperwork is complete, but the client is frightened. What does the nurse need to learn first?
questions.hintStrategy: When a vulnerable client shows distress, choose assessment at the client’s level before proceeding, restraining, or canceling.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 26-year-old veteran who returned from deployment 4 months ago comes to the clinic for an ankle sprain. During intake he says he has nightmares, avoids crowds, and has been drinking more to sleep. He adds, “Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask him directly whether he is thinking about killing himself
Give him information about local veterans’ support groups
Screen him for PTSD with the clinic’s standardized tool
Teach him how alcohol worsens sleep quality and mood
optionRationales: Correct. His statement is a warning sign; asking directly about suicide establishes his immediate safety.
Incorrect. Referral is helpful but does not address possible immediate risk.
Incorrect. Screening fits his symptoms but is not the priority after a hint of self-harm.
Incorrect. Teaching follows once his safety is established.
questions.rationale: Veterans returning from deployment are a vulnerable group with high rates of PTSD, and his statement that others would be better off without him is a warning sign of suicide risk. Safety comes first, so the nurse asks directly about suicidal thoughts; asking does not plant the idea and guides immediate action. PTSD screening is the tempting answer because his symptoms fit and guidelines support screening, but it is not the priority when he has just hinted at self-harm. Support groups and alcohol teaching follow once his safety is established.
questions.takeaway: When a vulnerable client hints at self-harm, ask directly about suicide before screening, teaching, or referral.
questions.hintContent: One statement in the stem signals a safety risk. Which one?
questions.hintStrategy: Safety outranks screening and teaching; when a stem includes a possible self-harm cue, address it first.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with COPD, type 2 diabetes, and early Alzheimer disease is being discharged home after pneumonia. The nurse reviews the discharge information shown in the exhibit. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Reteach inhaler technique and confirm understanding with teach-back
Give the client a list of local taxi services and discharge as planned
Document that the client may not adhere to the discharge plan
