Notify the case manager about her transportation and cost barriers
optionRationales: Incorrect. The exhibit shows teach-back is already correct; knowledge is not the barrier.
Incorrect. A taxi list ignores the cost barrier and may be unaffordable.
Incorrect. Labeling the client blames her for a system barrier and solves nothing.
Correct. Both barriers need team resources, such as rides and medication assistance, before discharge.

rows: Pulmonology clinic in 1 week, 40 miles away
“I don’t drive anymore, and I can’t pay for the new inhaler this month.”
Inhaler technique: teach-back completed and correct

questions.rationale: Dual-eligible clients are among the sickest and poorest and face high barriers to follow-through. The exhibit shows two unresolved barriers, no transportation to a distant follow-up and no money for a new inhaler, so the priority is engaging the case manager before discharge to arrange rides, medication assistance, or alternatives such as telehealth. Reteaching is tempting because teaching is a core nursing action, but the exhibit shows teach-back is already correct. A taxi list ignores cost, and labeling the client nonadherent blames her for a system problem.
questions.takeaway: Before discharging a vulnerable client, resolve access barriers with the case manager; teaching alone does not fix cost or transportation.
questions.hintContent: Which rows of the exhibit show a problem that is still unsolved?
questions.hintStrategy: In exhibit items, eliminate actions the exhibit shows are already complete, then match the remaining problem to the right team member.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 9-year-old is admitted for the third time this year with an asthma exacerbation. The provider’s note says, “Family nonadherent with controller inhaler.” The child’s mother works two jobs and became quiet when the inhaler was mentioned. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the mother what makes the daily inhaler hard for her to manage
Reteach the mother how to use the controller inhaler with a spacer
Report the family to child protective services for medical neglect
Document that the family has not followed the medication plan
optionRationales: Correct. An open question can uncover barriers such as cost, access, or schedules that the team can address.
Incorrect. This assumes the problem is knowledge rather than resources.
Incorrect. Reporting before assessing barriers harms the family and does not help the child.
Incorrect. Documentation alone labels the family without solving the problem.
questions.rationale: Advocacy for children begins with assessing the family’s needs, resources, and health literacy before labeling them. Asking an open question about barriers may reveal cost, pharmacy access, or work schedules that the team can address. Reteaching technique is tempting because it is a common nursing fix, but it assumes the problem is knowledge rather than resources. Reporting neglect or documenting nonadherence before understanding the barrier does not help the child.
questions.takeaway: Before labeling a family nonadherent, assess barriers such as cost, access, and health literacy.
questions.hintContent: The mother’s silence is a cue. What might she be unable to say without being asked?
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act: choose the open question that uncovers the barrier before options that teach, report, or document.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse has just finished teaching a 70-year-old client with newly diagnosed heart failure about daily weights. The client nods and says, “Okay, I’ve got it.” Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Give the client a printed handout on heart failure to review at home
Document that the client verbalized understanding of daily weights
Ask the client to explain when to weigh and which changes to report
Ask the client, “Do you have any questions about weighing yourself?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A handout adds information but does not check what was learned.
Incorrect. Nothing has yet been verified; a nod is not verbalized understanding.
Correct. Teach-back in the client’s own words is the best check of understanding.
Incorrect. A yes-or-no question rarely reveals gaps in understanding.
questions.rationale: Teach-back, in which the client explains or demonstrates in their own words, is the best check of understanding and a core empowerment tool. A nod and “I’ve got it” do not show that the client knows when to weigh, what change to report, or whom to call. Documenting understanding is the tempting answer, but nothing has yet been verified. Asking whether the client has questions invites a yes-or-no answer that rarely reveals gaps.
questions.takeaway: Confirm teaching with teach-back; a nod or “I’ve got it” is not evidence of understanding.
questions.hintContent: How can the nurse find out what the client actually learned?
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation-of-teaching items, choose the option in which the client demonstrates or explains, not the one in which the nurse asks a closed question.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A 49-year-old client newly diagnosed with breast cancer tells the nurse she joined an open online forum where members urge stopping chemotherapy in favor of high-dose vitamin infusions. She says she wants support from other women. Which action by the nurse best supports empowerment?
options: Advise her to stop using the internet for health information altogether
Tell her that support groups help less than talking with her oncologist
Encourage her to stay in the open forum, since peer support is important
Suggest a hospital-run online support group for women with breast cancer
optionRationales: Incorrect. Banning information sources is paternalistic and ignores her need.
Incorrect. This dismisses her stated need for connection with other women.
Incorrect. This forum promotes abandoning effective treatment.
Correct. This meets her need for peer support while steering her toward safe, accurate information.
questions.rationale: Empowerment builds the client’s knowledge and confidence while steering her toward safe, accurate support. A hospital-run group meets her real need for connection with other women while reducing exposure to harmful misinformation. Encouraging the open forum is tempting because peer support helps coping, but this forum promotes abandoning effective treatment. Banning internet use or dismissing support groups is paternalistic and ignores her stated need.
questions.takeaway: Empower clients by meeting their stated need through safe, credible resources rather than banning or dismissing.
questions.hintContent: Her need is valid; the source is the problem. Which option keeps the need and changes the source?
questions.hintStrategy: When a client’s goal is reasonable but the method is risky, choose the option that preserves the goal with a safer method.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client in a clinical trial of a new antihypertensive tells the research nurse, “The side effects are making me miserable, but I’m afraid that if I quit the study, the clinic will stop seeing me.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “You signed a consent form, so you should finish the study as agreed.”
“Let’s keep going for now; most side effects improve after a few weeks.”
“You can leave the study at any time and keep your regular care.”
“I’ll ask the study doctor whether you are allowed to withdraw early.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Signing does not bind a participant to continue.
Incorrect. Urging her to continue pressures a participant whose consent may no longer be voluntary.
Correct. Research participation is voluntary throughout, and withdrawal carries no penalty.
Incorrect. This implies permission is needed to withdraw, which is false.
questions.rationale: Research participation must stay voluntary, so a participant may withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of the care she would otherwise receive. Correcting her misunderstanding restores her ability to choose freely, and the nurse then reports the side effects to the investigator. Asking the study doctor whether she is allowed to withdraw is tempting because it involves the team, but it implies permission is needed. Urging her to continue pressures a participant whose consent may no longer be voluntary.
questions.takeaway: Research consent is ongoing; participants may withdraw at any time without losing regular care.
questions.hintContent: Her fear rests on a misunderstanding. What fact would free her to choose?
questions.hintStrategy: When a client’s choice is driven by a false belief, choose the response that corrects it accurately.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 67-year-old client tells the nurse, “If I can’t speak for myself, I want my daughter to decide for me. And I never want a feeding tube.” She asks which documents would accomplish both goals. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “A living will names your daughter and lists the treatments you would refuse.”
“A do-not-resuscitate order will cover the feeding tube and your daughter’s role.”
“A health care power of attorney names her; a living will states your tube wishes.”
“A health care power of attorney lets your daughter decide for you starting now.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A living will states treatment wishes; it does not name an agent.
Incorrect. A DNR order addresses only CPR.
Correct. One document names the agent; the other records treatment wishes.
Incorrect. The agent decides only when the client lacks capacity.
questions.rationale: A durable power of attorney for health care names a person, the agent, who makes decisions only when the client lacks capacity, while a living will states which life-sustaining treatments the client wants or refuses. Using both meets her two goals. The tempting error is thinking the agent’s authority starts immediately; while the client has capacity, she decides for herself. A DNR order addresses only CPR, not tube feeding or who decides. In North Carolina these are the Health Care Power of Attorney and the Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death.
questions.takeaway: A power of attorney for health care names a person; a living will states wishes. One does not replace the other.
questions.hintContent: She has two goals: naming a person and stating a treatment wish. Which documents match each?
questions.hintStrategy: For look-alike documents, ask “does this name someone or state something?” and match each option.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client with heart failure has the orders shown in the exhibit. This morning her temperature is 101.8°F (38.8°C), she has new crackles in the right lower lobe, and her oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. A newly hired nurse says, “Since she’s DNR, we probably shouldn’t call about this.” Which response by the precepting nurse is most appropriate?
options: “You’re right; with a DNR order, comfort measures are her only care now.”
“DNR means no CPR; let’s apply oxygen per the order and call the provider.”
“Let’s ask her daughter whether she wants treatment before we call.”
“We can call, but clients with DNR orders don’t usually get antibiotics.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. DNR does not mean comfort-only care; other treatment continues.
Correct. A DNR order limits CPR only; her new findings need oxygen and prompt provider evaluation.
Incorrect. Reporting a change in condition does not require family permission.
Incorrect. Antibiotics and other treatments continue unless the client or surrogate declines them.

rows: Do not resuscitate (DNR): no CPR, no intubation
Out of bed to chair with assistance
Titrate to keep SpO2 92% or higher

questions.rationale: A DNR order means no CPR; it does not mean do not treat. This client has new fever, crackles, and low oxygen saturation, suggesting pneumonia, so she should receive oxygen per the existing order, and the provider should be notified for evaluation and treatment. Assuming DNR means comfort-only care is the tempting error and can lead to undertreatment of vulnerable clients. Family input is not required to report a change in condition, and treatments such as antibiotics continue unless the client or her surrogate declines them.
questions.takeaway: DNR means no CPR, not “do not treat”; report changes and continue all other wanted care.
questions.hintContent: Read exactly what the code status order limits. Does it mention antibiotics or oxygen?
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem includes a code status, read its exact limits; do not extend a DNR order to treatments it does not name.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: Two months ago, a nurse taught a 55-year-old client with hypertension to use a home blood pressure monitor linked to a mobile app. Which statement by the client best shows that empowerment goals have been met?
options: “My daughter checks my pressure and lets me know if something is wrong.”
“When readings rose, I cut salt and called when they stayed high.”
“I check my pressure when I remember, usually when I have a headache.”
“I don’t look at the app much; I just wait for the nurse to call me.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Relying on a family member shows the client is not managing her own care.
Correct. Recognizing a trend, adjusting behavior, and seeking help shows self-efficacy and health literacy.
Incorrect. Checking only with symptoms misses the purpose of routine monitoring.
Incorrect. Waiting for the nurse shows passive reliance rather than partnership.
questions.rationale: Empowerment aims for self-efficacy, self-awareness, coping skills, and health literacy, so the client believes she can manage her health and acts on information. Recognizing a trend, adjusting behavior, and calling when readings stay high shows she is using the app as intended. Having a daughter monitor is tempting because family support is valuable, but it shows the client is not managing her own care. Checking only with symptoms or waiting for calls shows passive reliance rather than partnership.
questions.takeaway: Empowerment is shown when the client monitors, interprets, acts, and knows when to seek help.
questions.hintContent: Which client is using the information to take action herself?
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation items, choose the statement that shows the client independently doing the target behavior.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A pediatric nurse on a hospital policy committee learns that children on the unit are routinely awakened at night for nonurgent vital signs, the playroom closes on weekends, and many children leave meals uneaten. Which proposal best reflects advocacy for hospitalized children?
options: Cluster night care, open the playroom daily, and offer child-friendly meals
Add a parenting class so families can learn to manage their children’s behavior
Request standing sedative orders so that children sleep through the night
Ask parents to bring toys from home so the playroom can stay closed
optionRationales: Correct. These changes protect rest, play, and nutrition, which children need to heal and develop.
Incorrect. This shifts the problem to parents instead of fixing unit practices.
Incorrect. Sedation adds risk and treats a system problem with medication.
Incorrect. This shifts the burden to families, some with limited resources.
questions.rationale: Nurses advocate for children at the organizational level by serving on committees that protect play, rest, and good nutrition, which are essential to healing and development. Clustering care protects sleep, an open playroom supports normal development and coping, and child-friendly food improves intake. Asking parents to supply toys is tempting because it seems practical, but it shifts the burden to families, some with limited resources. Sedation for sleep adds risk and treats a system problem with medication.
questions.takeaway: Advocacy for hospitalized children means changing unit practices to protect rest, play, and nutrition.
questions.hintContent: Three problems appear in the stem. Which proposal fixes all three at the unit level?
questions.hintStrategy: For committee or policy items, choose the option that changes the system rather than shifting the burden to clients or families.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: An 81-year-old client with memory problems is admitted for dizziness. She tells the nurse she takes “just a water pill,” but her pharmacy fill history, shown in the exhibit, lists more. Her health care agent is her nephew, who fills her weekly pillbox. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Record only the water pill, because the client is the primary source
Verify her medication history with her nephew and the pharmacy record
Ask the client to describe each pill in her pillbox by color and shape
Hold all of her home medications until she can recall her own regimen
optionRationales: Incorrect. Her account conflicts with records, so it cannot stand alone.
Correct. Her recall is unreliable, so the nurse confirms with the person who manages her medications and with records.
Incorrect. This relies on the same unreliable memory.
Incorrect. The nurse cannot hold medications without a provider order.
questions.rationale: A rapid advocacy assessment includes judging how reliable the history is, especially when memory problems are present. Because her account conflicts with the pharmacy record, the nurse verifies with the person who manages her medications and with records, which may reveal a cause of her dizziness, such as the sedative and antihypertensives. Treating the client as the primary source is usually correct, which makes that option tempting, but here her recall is unreliable. Asking her to describe pills relies on the same memory, and the nurse cannot hold medications without an order.
questions.takeaway: When memory problems make the history unreliable, verify with the caregiver or agent and with records.
questions.hintContent: The exhibit and the client disagree. Who else can give an accurate picture?
questions.hintStrategy: When data conflict, choose the option that verifies with a reliable second source.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a 62-year-old client who will undergo a cardiac catheterization this afternoon. Which actions are within the nurse’s role in the informed consent process? Select all that apply.
options: Asking the client to describe the procedure in his own words
Explaining the risks, benefits, and alternatives of the procedure
Notifying the cardiologist when the client has unanswered questions
Obtaining consent from his spouse because he seems nervous
Documenting concerns about the client’s understanding
Witnessing that the signature on the form is the client’s own
optionRationales: Correct. Verifying understanding is a core nursing responsibility.
Incorrect. The provider performing the procedure explains it and obtains consent.
Correct. Unanswered questions mean consent is not yet informed; the provider must answer them.
Incorrect. Nervousness does not remove capacity; a capable client consents for himself.
Correct. Objective documentation of concerns is part of the nurse’s role.
Correct. The nurse witnesses that the client signed and appeared capable and willing.
questions.rationale: In informed consent, the provider who performs the procedure explains it, including risks, benefits, and alternatives, and obtains consent. The nurse verifies understanding, capacity, and free choice, witnesses the signature, reports concerns to the provider, and documents. Explaining the risks is the most tempting wrong choice because nurses teach constantly, but supplying consent information is the provider’s duty. Anxiety alone does not shift consent to a spouse.
questions.takeaway: Provider explains and obtains consent; nurse verifies, witnesses, reports concerns, and documents.
questions.hintContent: Sort each action into “provider’s job” or “nurse’s job.”
questions.hintStrategy: For role-based SATA items, picture who would be legally responsible for each action.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is planning self-management support for a 64-year-old client with type 2 diabetes and heart failure who lives on a farm 60 miles from the clinic, reads at a 6th-grade level, and owns a smartphone. Which tools are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Text-message reminders to take medications
Telehealth visits to set self-care plans and goals
Weekly in-person clinic visits to review every reading
A comprehensive 40-page manual given all at once
A short illustrated booklet written at his reading level
A mobile app to log daily weights and glucose readings
optionRationales: Correct. Texts support adherence and check-ins.
Correct. Telehealth reduces travel and supports goal-setting for rural clients.
Incorrect. Weekly 120-mile round trips are a barrier, not support.
Incorrect. Large amounts of information at once overwhelm a client with limited literacy.
Correct. Matching written material to literacy supports self-management he can reread.
Correct. Apps allow real-time self-monitoring on a device he already owns.
questions.rationale: Empowerment tools should fit the client’s literacy, location, and resources. Telehealth, mobile apps, texts, and short booklets at his reading level support self-monitoring and goal-setting without long trips. A comprehensive manual is tempting because it seems thorough, but large, complex materials overwhelm clients with limited health literacy; teaching works best in plain language and small chunks. Weekly in-person visits ignore the distance barrier.
questions.takeaway: Choose empowerment tools that match the client’s literacy, distance, and technology access.
questions.hintContent: Check each tool against three facts in the stem: distance, reading level, and smartphone.
questions.hintStrategy: For individualized-plan SATA items, eliminate options that conflict with any client-specific detail in the stem.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A nurse is evaluating a 34-year-old client with type 1 diabetes 3 months after an empowerment-focused education program. Which client statements indicate growth in empowerment? Select all that apply.
options: “I noticed my sugar drops when I skip lunch, so I pack a snack now.”
“I just do whatever the doctor says; I don’t need to understand it.”
“I feel confident I can handle sick days using my written plan.”
“I looked up my A1C on the portal and asked my provider what it means.”
“My husband handles my insulin so I don’t have to think about it.”
optionRationales: Correct. Recognizing personal patterns and acting on them reflects self-awareness.
Incorrect. Passive compliance reflects paternalism, not empowerment.
Correct. Confidence in managing a challenge reflects self-efficacy.
Correct. Finding and seeking to understand health information reflects health literacy.
Incorrect. Handing off self-management shows the client has not built skills or confidence.
questions.rationale: The EMPATHIE framework describes empowerment as self-efficacy, self-awareness, confidence, coping skills, and health literacy. Statements showing pattern recognition, confidence with sick-day management, and seeking to understand results demonstrate growth in these areas. Letting a spouse handle insulin is tempting because family support is valuable, but it shows the client is not building her own skills. Doing whatever the doctor says without understanding is the paternalistic model that empowerment replaces.
questions.takeaway: Empowerment shows as self-awareness, self-efficacy, and health literacy, not passive compliance.
questions.hintContent: Which statements show the client knowing, believing in, or acting on her own health information?
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation SATA items, select statements in which the client is the active agent.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A home health nurse in North Carolina visits a 37-year-old client with cerebral palsy who depends on a caregiver for meals and repositioning. The nurse finds a stage 3 sacral pressure injury and an empty refrigerator, and the client says, “She keeps my disability check and leaves for days.” Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Confront the caregiver and demand that she return the money
Wait until the next visit to see whether the situation improves
Assess the client’s wound, hydration, and nutrition status now
Document the findings and the client’s statements objectively
Report the situation to the county department of social services
Notify the home health agency supervisor of the situation
optionRationales: Incorrect. Confrontation can increase danger and is investigation, not the nurse’s role.
Incorrect. Delay leaves a dependent adult in danger; suspicion is enough to report.
Correct. Immediate physical needs come first for a dependent client.
Correct. Objective documentation, including his own words, supports protection.
Correct. Anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to DSS.
Correct. The supervisor supports the response and follow-up, in addition to the required report.
questions.rationale: A dependent adult with a serious pressure injury, no food, and financial exploitation needs immediate assessment and protection. Adult protective services, through the county department of social services in North Carolina, must receive a report from the person who suspects the need, and good-faith reporters are protected. Objective documentation and notifying the agency supervisor support the response but do not replace the report. Confronting the caregiver is tempting because it seems protective, but it can increase danger and turns the nurse into an investigator.
questions.takeaway: Suspected neglect or exploitation of a disabled adult: meet urgent needs, report to adult protective services, and document objectively.
questions.hintContent: Which actions protect the client now and fulfill the legal duty to report?
questions.hintStrategy: In abuse and neglect SATA items, reject options that confront, investigate, or delay.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A 16-year-old who is not emancipated comes to a North Carolina health department without a parent. For which services may this adolescent give her own consent? Select all that apply.
options: Tubal sterilization
Testing and treatment for chlamydia
Prenatal care for a confirmed pregnancy
Elective removal of a benign mole for cosmetic reasons
Outpatient treatment for alcohol use
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sterilization is specifically excluded from minor consent.
Correct. Minors may consent to diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infections.
Correct. Minors may consent to pregnancy-related care other than sterilization or abortion.
Incorrect. Routine elective procedures require parental consent for an unemancipated minor.
Correct. Minors may consent to treatment for substance or alcohol abuse.
questions.rationale: Minors generally cannot consent to their own care, but laws create exceptions so adolescents do not avoid treatment for sensitive conditions. In North Carolina, a minor may consent to care for sexually transmitted and other reportable diseases, pregnancy (not sterilization or abortion), substance or alcohol abuse, and emotional disturbance. Sterilization is the tempting choice because it relates to reproductive care, but it is specifically excluded. Elective cosmetic procedures require a parent’s consent for an unemancipated minor.
questions.takeaway: Minors may consent to STI, pregnancy, substance use, and mental health care, but not sterilization or routine elective procedures.
questions.hintContent: Which services might a teen avoid altogether if parental consent were required?
questions.hintStrategy: For minor-consent items, look for sensitive services tied to public health; reject permanent or elective procedures.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse at an urban community clinic is planning outreach. Which clients belong to groups the nurse should recognize as vulnerable populations needing extra advocacy? Select all that apply.
options: A 45-year-old man recently released from prison with no health insurance
A 40-year-old engineer with employer insurance and no chronic illness
A 52-year-old teacher who drives herself to her yearly checkups
A 74-year-old dual-eligible client with Alzheimer disease and COPD
A 30-year-old woman with a disability who earns $13,000 a year
optionRationales: Correct. Incarceration history and lack of insurance limit resources and raise risk.
Incorrect. Stable resources and no risk factors do not place him in a vulnerable group.
Incorrect. Access to care and transportation suggest no added vulnerability.
Correct. Dual-eligible clients are among the sickest and poorest.
Correct. People with disabilities often have low income and face added barriers.
questions.rationale: Vulnerable populations are groups at higher risk of disease, disability, and early death because of a lack of resources, risk factors, or both. Dual-eligible clients, people leaving incarceration without coverage, and people with disabilities and low income all fit this definition. The clients with stable insurance and transportation are tempting to include because everyone deserves advocacy, but they lack the added risk that calls for targeted outreach. Recognizing vulnerability helps the nurse direct resources where barriers are greatest.
questions.takeaway: Vulnerability comes from limited resources, added risk factors, or both; target extra advocacy there.
questions.hintContent: For each client, look for missing resources or added health risks.
questions.hintStrategy: In classification SATA items, apply the definition to each option; select only those that meet it.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse begins a rapid advocacy assessment for a 59-year-old client just diagnosed with lung cancer who will meet with the oncologist tomorrow. Which data should the nurse collect? Select all that apply.
options: Whether the family agrees with the client’s likely choice
How the client is coping with the news
The client’s health literacy
Who the client relies on for support at home
Which treatment the nurse personally believes is best
What the client understands about the diagnosis and plan
optionRationales: Incorrect. Family agreement is not required for a capable client’s decision.
Correct. Coping influences readiness to make decisions.
Correct. Health literacy shapes how information should be given.
Correct. The support system affects coping and planning.
Incorrect. The nurse’s preference is not assessment data and risks paternalism.
Correct. Understanding is the starting point for any advocacy.
questions.rationale: Advocacy follows the nursing process and starts with a rapid assessment of the client’s understanding, health literacy, support system, and coping, followed by capacity and reliability of the history. These data tell the nurse how to inform, whom to involve, and what help the client needs before a major decision. Family agreement is the tempting distractor because family matters, but a capable client’s decision does not depend on it. The nurse’s own preference is not assessment data.
questions.takeaway: Advocacy assessment: understanding, health literacy, support, coping, then capacity and reliability.
questions.hintContent: Which data are about the client, and which are about other people’s views?
questions.hintStrategy: For assessment SATA items, select data that describe the client’s own situation and abilities.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A 70-year-old widower is being discharged after a stroke. He lives alone in a second-floor apartment, no longer drives, worries about paying rent, and takes warfarin along with a newly prescribed antibiotic. Which referrals should the nurse request? Select all that apply.
options: Case manager to arrange transportation and home support
Social worker to explore financial assistance resources
The state protection and advocacy agency to investigate abuse
A local NAMI affiliate for family education about mental illness
Pharmacist to review the warfarin and antibiotic for interactions
optionRationales: Correct. Case managers coordinate rides and home services.
Correct. Social workers address money concerns that threaten safety at home.
Incorrect. Nothing in the stem suggests abuse or a rights violation.
Incorrect. NAMI supports people affected by mental illness, which is not his current need.
Correct. Antibiotics can interact with warfarin; the pharmacist can review the regimen.
questions.rationale: Interprofessional collaboration links the client to the person best suited for each need. The case manager handles transportation and home support, the pharmacist reviews the warfarin and antibiotic for interactions, and the social worker addresses financial strain. The protection and advocacy agency is tempting because the client is vulnerable, but it investigates abuse and rights violations, which are not present here. NAMI serves people and families affected by mental illness.
questions.takeaway: Match each barrier to the right team member: case manager for rides and home help, pharmacist for drugs, social worker for money.
questions.hintContent: List the client’s problems, then match each to a professional.
questions.hintStrategy: For referral SATA items, select only referrals that match a problem stated in the stem.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 0200, a nurse sees a colleague at the medication cart drawing up IV hydromorphone for a postoperative client. The colleague’s pupils are pinpoint, her speech is slow, and she nods off briefly while labeling the syringe. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Wait until the colleague’s break to talk with her privately about drug use
Report the colleague to the state board of nursing at the end of the shift
Ask the colleague to hand over the syringe and notify the charge nurse now
Watch the colleague give the dose to confirm whether she is impaired
optionRationales: Incorrect. Waiting lets an impaired nurse give a high-alert opioid.
Incorrect. A later board report does not protect this client now and normally follows the supervisor report.
Correct. This stops imminent harm to the client and reports to the direct supervisor at once.
Incorrect. Suspicion is enough; watching allows harm to occur.
questions.rationale: When impairment threatens a client right now, the first step is to stop the harm by taking the medication out of the impaired nurse’s hands, and then to notify the direct supervisor immediately. Suspicion is enough; the nurse does not need proof or a confession. Reporting to the board is tempting because impairment on duty is a conduct issue, but a board report later does not protect this client now. Waiting or watching allows an impaired nurse to give a high-alert opioid.
questions.takeaway: Stop the harm first, then tell the direct supervisor; outside reports follow.
questions.hintContent: Harm is seconds away. What has to happen before anything else?
questions.hintStrategy: When an impaired person is about to give care, choose the option that both stops the act and reaches the supervisor.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: Near the end of a shift, a colleague approaches a nurse with an empty syringe and says, “I wasted half a milligram of hydromorphone earlier. Can you cosign it in the system? I’m in a hurry.” This is the third such request from the colleague this week. What should the nurse do first?
options: Decline to cosign, because the nurse did not witness the waste
Cosign the waste, since the colleague is experienced and trusted
Cosign this time, and then report the pattern to the charge nurse
Ask the colleague to explain where the rest of the drug went
optionRationales: Correct. Cosigning attests to a waste the nurse saw; signing without seeing it is falsification.
Incorrect. Trust does not replace witnessing; this can conceal diversion.
Incorrect. Reporting is needed, but cosigning still creates a false record.
Incorrect. Questioning the colleague is investigation, which belongs to supervisors and pharmacy.
questions.rationale: Cosigning a waste attests that the nurse watched the drug being discarded, so signing for a waste not witnessed is falsification and can conceal diversion. The first action is to refuse, and the repeated pattern of unwitnessed wastes is then reported promptly to the supervisor. Cosigning and then reporting is tempting because it includes a report, but it still creates a false record. Questioning the colleague turns the nurse into an investigator.
questions.takeaway: Never cosign a controlled-substance waste you did not see; refuse, then report the pattern.
questions.hintContent: What exactly does a cosignature on a waste certify?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any option that requires the nurse to document something false, even if it is paired with a good action.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse reports to the charge nurse that a colleague smells strongly of alcohol and stumbled at the medication cart. The charge nurse replies, “We’re already two nurses short. Just keep an eye on her, and we’ll deal with it tomorrow.” What should the nurse do next?
options: Follow the charge nurse’s instructions and keep watching the colleague
Tell the colleague that she must leave the unit and go home now
Notify the house supervisor of the colleague’s condition right away
Email the nurse manager so the problem is handled tomorrow
optionRationales: Incorrect. Short staffing never justifies letting an impaired nurse care for clients.
Incorrect. Relieving her is a supervisor’s decision, and she may drive impaired.
Correct. When the direct supervisor does not act, the nurse goes to the next level immediately.
Incorrect. This follows the chain but delays action while clients are at risk.
questions.rationale: When the direct supervisor does not act on an unsafe situation, the nurse moves up the chain of command immediately; short staffing never justifies letting an impaired nurse care for clients. The house supervisor has authority to relieve the colleague and arrange coverage tonight. Emailing the manager is tempting because it follows the chain, but it delays action until tomorrow while clients remain at risk. Sending the colleague home is the supervisor’s decision, and she may drive impaired.
questions.takeaway: If the supervisor does not act on imminent risk, go to the next level now, not tomorrow.
questions.hintContent: The first report went nowhere. Who is the next level up who is available tonight?
questions.hintStrategy: For chain-of-command items, choose the next level that can act now; reject options that delay or skip levels.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse scrolling social media sees that a coworker has posted an X-ray of a foreign object in a client’s abdomen with the caption, “You won’t believe what we pulled out tonight!” No name appears, but the hospital and date are tagged. What should the nurse do first?
options: Comment publicly on the post asking the coworker to delete it now
Report the post to the nurse manager or the hospital privacy officer
Take no action, because the client’s name does not appear in the post
Share a screenshot in the unit group chat to warn the other staff
optionRationales: Incorrect. A public comment draws attention to the breach and leaves it unreported.
Correct. Identifying details make this a privacy breach that must be reported promptly.
Incorrect. An image with a date and location can identify a client without a name.
Incorrect. Sharing spreads the protected information further.
questions.rationale: Any detail that could identify a client, such as an image, a date, or a location, makes a post a privacy breach even without a name. The nurse reports promptly to the supervisor or privacy officer, who can act to remove it and follow policy and law. Publicly commenting is tempting because it seems to fix the problem quickly, but it draws more attention to the breach and leaves it unreported. Sharing a screenshot spreads the protected information further.
questions.takeaway: A client image or identifying detail online is a privacy breach even without a name; report it, don’t spread it.
questions.hintContent: Could someone who knows the client recognize the case from this post?
questions.hintStrategy: For privacy breach items, choose the formal report; reject options that ignore, amplify, or handle it informally.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the order shown in the exhibit for a 76-year-old client with atrial fibrillation and calls the prescriber, who says, “Just give it. I know what I ordered.” What should the nurse do next?
options: Give the dose as ordered, since the prescriber has confirmed it
Give 0.25 mg instead, which is the dose the client usually receives
Report the prescriber to the state medical board after the shift
Hold the dose and take the concern to the charge nurse right away
optionRationales: Incorrect. A prescriber’s insistence does not make a tenfold dose safe.
Incorrect. Changing a dose without an order is outside the nurse’s scope.
Incorrect. A later report does not protect the client now and skips the chain.
Correct. An unsafe order the prescriber will not change is held and escalated.
questions.rationale: The new order is ten times the client’s usual digoxin dose, and a nurse who gives a medication she believes is unsafe shares responsibility for the harm. After the prescriber refuses to change it, the nurse holds the dose and uses the chain of command, starting with the charge nurse. Giving the dose because the prescriber confirmed it is the tempting answer, but insistence does not make an unsafe dose safe. Changing the dose on her own is outside her scope, and a later board report does not protect the client now.
questions.takeaway: For an unsafe order the prescriber will not change: hold it and go up the chain of command.
questions.hintContent: Compare the new dose with the doses on the MAR.
questions.hintStrategy: When the provider has already been contacted, the next step is the next level of the chain, not compliance and not a solo fix.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: On a memory care unit, a nurse hears shouting and finds a nursing assistant gripping a resident’s wrist tightly and saying, “Stop fighting me or you won’t get dinner,” while the resident cries and tries to pull away from her bath. What should the nurse do first?
options: Report the nursing assistant to the nurse manager at the end of the shift
Step in, stop the bath, and stay with the resident to check for injury
Ask the nursing assistant to finish the bath more gently and calmly
Call adult protective services before speaking to anyone on the unit
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting is required, but not at the end of the shift and not before the resident is safe.
Correct. Protecting the resident from ongoing harm comes before reporting.
Incorrect. This leaves the resident with the person harming her.
Incorrect. An outside call leaves the resident in danger right now.
questions.rationale: Protecting the resident from immediate harm comes before reporting: the nurse steps in, stops the care, stays with the resident, and assesses for injury. Gripping her wrist and threatening to withhold food is abuse and coercion that serves staff convenience. Calling an outside agency is tempting because abuse must be reported, but it leaves the resident in danger right now. The supervisor and any required agencies are notified immediately after she is safe, not at the end of the shift.
questions.takeaway: Stop the abuse and protect the client first; then report to the supervisor and required agencies.
questions.hintContent: Is the resident safe at this moment?
questions.hintStrategy: When harm is happening in front of you, choose the option that stops it before any reporting option.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A 14-year-old tells the school nurse that her stepfather hits her with a belt when he drinks and shows bruises on her upper thighs. She begs, “Please don’t tell anyone. It will only make it worse.” What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Promise to keep her secret so she will continue to trust the nurse
Call the stepfather to hear his explanation of the bruises
Tell the principal and let the principal decide whether to report
Report the suspected abuse to county child protective services
optionRationales: Incorrect. The nurse cannot promise secrecy when a child may be abused.
Incorrect. Contacting the alleged abuser is investigation and may increase danger.
Incorrect. Telling a supervisor does not meet the nurse’s own duty to report.
Correct. The person who suspects child abuse must report it to the designated agency without waiting for proof.
questions.rationale: Suspected child abuse must be reported to the designated child protective services agency, in North Carolina the county department of social services, by the person who suspects it, without waiting for proof. The nurse cannot promise secrecy; she can explain honestly that she must get help to keep the student safe. Telling the principal is tempting because schools have reporting procedures, but notifying a supervisor does not meet the nurse’s own legal duty. Contacting the stepfather could increase the danger.
questions.takeaway: Report suspected child abuse yourself to child protective services; never promise secrecy or wait for proof.
questions.hintContent: Whose legal duty is it to report, and to whom?
questions.hintStrategy: For mandatory reporting items, choose the option that reports directly to the designated agency; reject options that delay, investigate, or hand off the duty.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A staff nurse is working with a nursing student during a clinical rotation. As the student prepares to give oral medications, the nurse notices an odor of alcohol on her breath and that she is unsteady at the medication cart. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Stop the student’s medication pass and notify her clinical instructor
Ask the student privately how much she had to drink before clinical
Let the student give the medications while the nurse watches closely
Report the student to the state board of nursing for impaired practice
optionRationales: Correct. This prevents harm and reaches the student’s direct supervisor.
Incorrect. Questioning her is investigation and delays protecting clients.
Incorrect. An impaired person should not give medications at all.
Incorrect. A board report is not the first step and does not protect clients now.
questions.rationale: The duty to report unsafe conduct covers everyone involved in client care, including students. The nurse first prevents harm by stopping the student from giving medications, then notifies the student’s direct supervisor, the clinical instructor, who can relieve her and follow school policy. Supervising closely is tempting because the nurse is present, but an impaired person should not give medications at all. Questioning her is investigating, and a board report is not the first step.
questions.takeaway: Impairment rules apply to students too: stop the care, then notify the student’s instructor.
questions.hintContent: Who is this student’s direct supervisor on the unit?
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the same stop-then-tell pattern to any team member, including students, aides, and providers.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: In the operating room, the circulating nurse notices that the surgeon scrubbing for an elective laminectomy smells of alcohol and is slurring words. The client has not yet been anesthetized. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the anesthesiologist to decide whether the surgeon is able to operate
Proceed with the case and report the surgeon after the procedure
Notify the perioperative charge nurse before anesthesia begins
Report the surgeon to the state medical board at the end of the day
optionRationales: Incorrect. This bypasses the nurse’s chain of command and places the decision with a peer.
Incorrect. Proceeding exposes the client to an impaired surgeon.
Correct. The direct supervisor can stop the case and involve medical leadership before harm occurs.
Incorrect. A later report does not protect this client now.
questions.rationale: The duty to report unsafe conduct applies to every member of the health care team, including physicians. Because the client has not yet been anesthetized, there is still time to prevent harm, so the nurse immediately notifies her direct supervisor, who can stop the case and involve medical leadership. Asking the anesthesiologist is tempting because he is a physician colleague, but it bypasses the nurse’s chain of command and makes him responsible for a decision that is not his. Proceeding and reporting later exposes the client to an impaired surgeon.
questions.takeaway: Impairment in any team member, including a physician, is reported to your supervisor immediately, before harm occurs.
questions.hintContent: Rank matters less than safety. Who is the nurse’s first report?
questions.hintStrategy: Do not let the impaired person’s title change the reporting pathway; the nurse still goes to her own supervisor first.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse reviewing controlled-substance records notices the pattern shown in the exhibit for a well-liked colleague. Today the colleague is drowsy, has pinpoint pupils, and is assigned to four postoperative clients. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Privately report the observations to the charge nurse right away
Ask the colleague about the pattern before reporting it to anyone
Keep tracking the records for another week to be certain
Search the colleague’s locker for missing hydromorphone vials
optionRationales: Correct. Clients are at risk now, and suspicion is enough to report to the supervisor.
Incorrect. Confronting delays protection and can lead to concealment.
Incorrect. Waiting for proof leaves clients at risk.
Incorrect. Searching is investigation that belongs to supervisors and pharmacy.
questions.rationale: Opioid doses for low pain scores, late or missing waste cosigns, and clients whose pain rises after documented doses suggest diversion, and drowsiness with pinpoint pupils suggests impairment today. Clients are at risk now, so the nurse privately reports the facts to the charge nurse immediately; suspicion is enough. Confronting the colleague is tempting because it feels fair, but it delays protection and can lead to concealment. Gathering more proof or searching belongings is investigation.
questions.takeaway: Suspected diversion with signs of impairment is reported to the supervisor immediately; do not confront, investigate, or wait for proof.
questions.hintContent: Look at the pain scores before and after each dose. What does the pattern suggest?
questions.hintStrategy: In diversion items, report suspicion to the supervisor; eliminate options that confront, investigate, or wait.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she just gave metoprolol 50 mg by mouth to the wrong client. Two clients with similar last names were moved into adjacent rooms this morning, and the unit’s barcode scanner has been broken for a week. What should the nurse do first?
options: Complete an incident report describing the error
Notify the nurse manager that the scanner is broken
Call the provider to report the medication error
Assess the client’s heart rate and blood pressure
optionRationales: Incorrect. An incident report is required but comes after the client is assessed.
Incorrect. Fixing the system matters but does not address this client’s safety.
Incorrect. The provider will need current vital signs to decide on treatment.
Correct. Client safety comes first; metoprolol can cause bradycardia and hypotension.
questions.rationale: After a medication error, the first priority is the client’s safety; metoprolol can cause bradycardia and hypotension, so the nurse assesses heart rate and blood pressure. The provider is then notified with assessment data, the incident report is completed, and the system problems are reported. Calling the provider is the tempting answer because it is required and urgent, but the provider will need current vital signs to decide on treatment. Under Just Culture, this is human error made likely by system factors, and an honest report helps fix the scanner and name alerts.
questions.takeaway: After a medication error, assess the client first, then notify the provider, then report.
questions.hintContent: What could this drug do to the client in the next hour?
questions.hintStrategy: When every option is a correct action, order them: assess the client, notify the provider, document, then fix the system.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: On the day of discharge, a 72-year-old client who was on the unit for 3 weeks hands the nurse a box containing an expensive watch and says, “You were like a daughter to me. Please take it.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Thank you so much. I’ll wear it every day and think of you.”
“I can accept it if you don’t tell anyone else on the unit.”
“That’s so kind, but I can’t accept it. Caring for you was a privilege.”
“Please give it to my manager, and she will decide what we should do with it.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Accepting a valuable gift benefits the nurse and is a boundary violation.
Incorrect. Secrecy is a hallmark of boundary violations.
Correct. Declining kindly keeps the boundary while honoring the client’s feelings.
Incorrect. This avoids the nurse’s own duty to keep the boundary.
questions.rationale: Accepting money or valuable gifts from a client is a boundary violation because it benefits the nurse and can exploit the client’s gratitude or dependence. The nurse declines kindly while acknowledging the client’s feelings, which keeps the relationship therapeutic. Passing the decision to the manager is tempting because it seems cautious, but it avoids the nurse’s own responsibility to keep the boundary. Agreeing to keep the gift secret adds secrecy, a hallmark of boundary violations.
questions.takeaway: Decline valuable gifts kindly; the nurse, not the client, keeps the boundary.
questions.hintContent: Whose need would be met by accepting the watch?
questions.hintStrategy: For boundary items, choose the response that holds the limit warmly; reject options that accept, hide, or pass the decision on.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: To save time, a nurse gives an IV heparin bolus to a client before the prescriber writes the order. Earlier, the pharmacist and the charge nurse both told her not to give heparin without an order. The client is unharmed. Using a Just Culture framework, how is this behavior best classified?
options: Human error, managed by consoling the nurse
At-risk behavior, managed by coaching the nurse
No concern, because the client was not harmed
Reckless behavior, managed with discipline
optionRationales: Incorrect. Human error is an unintended slip, not a deliberate choice after warnings.
Incorrect. At-risk behavior occurs when the risk is not recognized, not after explicit warnings.
Incorrect. Just Culture judges the choice, not the outcome.
Correct. Knowingly disregarding a substantial risk after warnings is reckless.
questions.rationale: Just Culture judges the choice the nurse made, not the outcome. Giving a high-alert medication without an order after two explicit warnings is a conscious disregard of a substantial, known risk, which defines reckless behavior and warrants discipline. At-risk behavior is the tempting choice because it also involves a shortcut, but at-risk behavior occurs when the risk is not recognized or is mistakenly believed justified, not after direct warnings. The absence of harm does not change the classification.
questions.takeaway: Just Culture: at-risk means the risk was not seen (coach); reckless means a known risk was ignored (discipline); the outcome does not decide it.
questions.hintContent: Did the nurse know the risk before acting?
questions.hintStrategy: For Just Culture items, ask two questions: was the act intended, and was the risk known?
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client treated for depression on an inpatient unit for 2 weeks tells the nurse on the day of discharge, “You’re the only one who really understands me. Can we keep in touch after I go home?” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Of course. Here’s my personal cell number; call me whenever you need to talk.”
“I’m glad I could help. Our work ends today, but your outpatient team will help.”
“Let’s connect on social media so I can see how you’re doing.”
“That isn’t allowed, so let’s not talk about it anymore.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Personal contact after discharge blurs boundaries with a vulnerable client.
Correct. This acknowledges the bond, states the limit, and connects the client to ongoing support.
Incorrect. Connecting online with a client creates a boundary violation risk.
Incorrect. Shutting down the conversation is nontherapeutic and leaves the client without support.
questions.rationale: The therapeutic relationship exists to meet the client’s needs and ends at discharge; personal contact afterward risks a boundary violation, especially with a vulnerable client. The best response acknowledges the bond, states the professional limit, and connects the client with ongoing support. Giving a phone number or connecting online is tempting because it seems caring, but it blurs boundaries. Shutting down the conversation is a communication block that leaves the client without a path to support.
questions.takeaway: Acknowledge the bond, state the professional limit, and connect the client to ongoing support.
questions.hintContent: The client needs support after discharge. Who should provide it?
questions.hintStrategy: In boundary communication items, the best answer is warm, honest about the limit, and offers an appropriate alternative.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: Two weeks after a nurse reported a colleague for suspected impairment on duty, the nurse manager shares how the situation was resolved. Which outcome best indicates that the report achieved its purpose?
options: She was quietly moved to night shift on a different unit
Staff on the unit agreed to keep the matter among themselves
Her clients were reassessed, and she entered monitored treatment
She apologized and promised that it would not happen again
optionRationales: Incorrect. A transfer moves the risk to other clients without treatment.
Incorrect. A private agreement is a cover-up that protects no one.
Correct. Client safety and help for the colleague are the two goals of reporting impairment.
Incorrect. A promise does not ensure treatment, monitoring, or client safety.
questions.rationale: Reporting impairment has two goals: protecting clients now and getting the colleague help, often through an alternative-to-discipline program that provides treatment and monitoring. Reassessed, safe clients and a colleague in monitored treatment show both goals were met. A quiet transfer is tempting because it removes her from the unit, but it moves the risk to other clients without treatment. A private agreement or an apology leaves clients and the colleague unprotected.
questions.takeaway: A good outcome after reporting impairment means clients are safe and the colleague is in treatment and monitoring.
questions.hintContent: What two things should reporting accomplish?
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation items, choose the option that meets every goal of the intervention, not just one.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A coworker pulls a nurse aside and says, “I’ve been keeping leftover oxycodone from wastes to get through my shifts. Please don’t tell anyone. I’ll get help on my own, I promise.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “I’ll keep this just between us as long as you start a treatment program this week.”
“If you stop taking it today, there’s no need to involve anyone else.”
“I can’t talk about this. You’ll need to deal with it on your own.”
“I care about you, and I must report this so clients are safe and you get help.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Agreeing to secrecy is covering up and leaves clients at risk.
Incorrect. Diversion is a conduct issue that must be reported regardless of promises.
Incorrect. Refusing to engage abandons a colleague in crisis and still fails to report.
Correct. This is compassionate and honest that reporting is required.
questions.rationale: A coworker’s admission of diversion is a conduct issue that endangers clients and the coworker, and the nurse must report it to the supervisor. The best response shows compassion while being honest that reporting is required; reporting often connects the nurse to an alternative-to-discipline program for treatment and monitoring. Agreeing to secrecy in exchange for treatment is tempting because it seems supportive, but it is covering up and leaves clients at risk. Refusing to engage abandons a colleague in crisis.
questions.takeaway: Loyalty to a coworker never outweighs client safety; respond with compassion and report.
questions.hintContent: Can a promise to get help replace the duty to report?
questions.hintStrategy: When a colleague asks for secrecy, choose the response that is both kind and honest about the duty to report.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A respiratory therapist arrives to give a nebulizer treatment to a client with asthma. The nurse notices that the therapist has slurred speech, an unsteady gait, and glassy eyes. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Keep the therapist from treating the client and notify the charge nurse
Allow the treatment, since the therapist is not under nursing supervision
Give the treatment herself and say nothing about the therapist
Contact the respiratory therapy manager on the next business day
optionRationales: Correct. The duty to report covers non-nurses; the client is protected and the supervisor is told.
Incorrect. The duty to report applies to anyone caring for clients.
Incorrect. This protects one client but leaves the therapist caring for others.
Incorrect. Delayed reporting leaves clients at risk now.
questions.rationale: The duty to report unsafe conduct applies to anyone caring for clients, not only nurses. The nurse protects the client by keeping the impaired therapist from providing care and promptly notifies her direct supervisor, who can involve respiratory therapy leadership and arrange a safe replacement. Assuming the therapist is someone else’s responsibility is the tempting error. Quietly giving the treatment herself may help this client but leaves the therapist caring for others, and next-day reporting delays protection.
questions.takeaway: The duty to report impairment covers every team member, not just nurses.
questions.hintContent: Does it matter which department the impaired person works for?
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the option that protects this client and every other client the person might reach.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing mandatory reporting with newly hired emergency department nurses in North Carolina. Which statement by a new nurse indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I don’t need to have proof of abuse before I make a report to social services.”
“A report made in good faith is protected even if abuse isn’t confirmed.”
“I’ll document what I observed and the child’s own words objectively.”
“If I suspect child abuse, I’ll let the charge nurse decide about calling DSS.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is correct; suspicion is enough to report.
Incorrect. This is correct; good-faith reporters are immune.
Incorrect. This is correct; objective documentation supports the report.
Correct. The nurse who suspects abuse must report it; a supervisor cannot decide for her.
questions.rationale: In North Carolina, consistent with the national standard, a person who suspects child maltreatment must report it to the designated child protective services agency, the county department of social services. The duty belongs to the nurse who suspects it; telling a supervisor may be required by policy, but it does not replace the report. The statement about not needing proof is accurate, though new nurses sometimes mistake it for an error. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability, and objective documentation of observations and the child’s words is correct.
questions.takeaway: Mandatory child abuse reports go from the person who suspects to child protective services; a supervisor cannot decide for you.
questions.hintContent: Whose duty is the report, and can it be handed to someone else?
questions.hintStrategy: For “needs further teaching” items, find the one false statement; true statements that sound surprising are not the answer.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old client with borderline personality disorder tells the day nurse that the night nurse touched her breasts while “checking her heart” and made comments about her body. Several staff members say, “She always makes up stories.” Which action by the nurse is most appropriate after listening to the client?
options: Ask the night nurse for his account before deciding whether to report
Reassure the client that the night nurse is professional and would not do that
Document her words objectively and report them to the nursing supervisor now
Wait to see whether other clients make similar reports about the nurse
optionRationales: Incorrect. Investigation belongs to supervisors and could put the client at risk.
Incorrect. This dismisses the client’s report.
Correct. A psychiatric diagnosis never makes an abuse report less credible; it is reported promptly.
Incorrect. Waiting leaves this client and others at risk.
questions.rationale: A psychiatric diagnosis never makes an abuse report less credible, and people with mental illness face a higher risk of abuse. The nurse documents the client’s own words objectively and reports promptly to the supervisor, who starts the investigation; sexual misconduct is a conduct issue that is also reported to the board of nursing. Hearing the accused nurse’s side first is tempting because it seems fair, but investigation belongs to supervisors, and contacting him could compromise the client’s safety. Dismissing her or waiting for more reports leaves her and others at risk.
questions.takeaway: Take every abuse allegation seriously regardless of diagnosis: document the client’s words and report to the supervisor at once.
questions.hintContent: Does the client’s diagnosis change the nurse’s duty?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that judge credibility, investigate, or wait; choose the one that documents and reports.

questions.stem: At 0630, a client with a head injury who required hourly neurologic checks tells the day nurse, “It was great; nobody woke me up all night.” The night nurse’s charting shows a check every hour. When asked, the night nurse says, “Everyone fills those in when it’s busy.” Which action by the day nurse is most appropriate?
options: Remind the night nurse to chart only what she does and let it go this time
Assess the client now and report the false charting to the charge nurse
Correct the night nurse’s entries in the record to show the missed checks
Report the night nurse directly to the state board of nursing this morning
optionRationales: Incorrect. Falsification is a conduct issue, not something to coach away privately.
Correct. The client needs a verified assessment, and falsified documentation is reported to the supervisor.
Incorrect. Editing another nurse’s entries is itself improper documentation.
Incorrect. The facility chain comes first; board reports follow per policy and law.
questions.rationale: Documenting assessments that were not done is falsification, a conduct issue that endangers clients because others rely on the record. The client with a head injury has gone hours without verified neurologic checks, so the nurse assesses him now and then reports the documentation concern to her direct supervisor. Reporting straight to the board is tempting because falsification is a board matter, but the facility chain of command comes first and the board report follows. Coaching privately or editing the entries leaves a false record in place.
questions.takeaway: Falsified documentation is a conduct issue: protect the client with a real assessment, then report to the supervisor.
questions.hintContent: Two problems exist: an unassessed client and a false record. Which option handles both?
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem hides a client-safety gap inside a conduct issue, look for the option that addresses the client first.

questions.stem: A nurse was interrupted three times while programming an IV pump and set a heparin infusion at 100 mL/hr instead of 10 mL/hr. She found the error within minutes, stopped the pump, and reported it. The client was unharmed. Which responses by the nurse manager are consistent with a Just Culture approach? Select all that apply.
options: Adding drug library limits to the pump to flag unsafe rates
Reviewing how interruptions during pump programming can be reduced
Reporting the nurse to the board of nursing for unsafe practice
Consoling the nurse and acknowledging her prompt report
Suspending the nurse without pay to deter future errors
optionRationales: Correct. System safeguards reduce the chance of repeat slips.
Correct. Fixing the system factors that made the error likely is the core response to human error.
Incorrect. A single human error is not a conduct issue for the board.
Correct. Human error is met with support, which encourages honest reporting.
Incorrect. Punishing an unintended slip discourages reporting.
questions.rationale: Just Culture classifies an unintended slip under distracting conditions as human error, and the response is to console the nurse and fix the system. Reducing interruptions and adding pump safeguards address the conditions that made the error likely. Suspension is tempting to managers who want accountability, but punishing human error makes nurses hide mistakes, and hidden errors repeat. Board reporting is reserved for conduct issues such as diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary violations, and privacy breaches.
questions.takeaway: Human error: console the nurse and fix the system; punishment drives errors underground.
questions.hintContent: Was this a choice to take a risk, or an accidental slip?
questions.hintStrategy: Classify the behavior first, then select only the responses that match that category.
questions.ref: Module 43 · Advocacy · Reporting Unprofessional Actions · pp. 2–3, 6–9

questions.stem: At 0900, the charge nurse relieves a nurse who appeared intoxicated after she had given morning medications to five clients. Which actions are appropriate next? Select all that apply.
options: Discussing the nurse’s condition with the whole unit at the noon huddle
Charting “impaired nurse gave meds” in each affected client’s record
Recording objective observations, with times, on an incident report
Reassessing the clients who received medications from her this morning
Arranging for the relieved nurse not to drive herself home
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sharing details with staff breaches the colleague’s confidentiality.
Incorrect. The client record holds client-care facts; it never mentions the incident or report.
Correct. Factual, timed observations belong in the incident report.
Correct. Medication errors may have occurred, so these clients need assessment.
Correct. An impaired person driving is a safety risk to her and others.
questions.rationale: After an impaired nurse is relieved, the priorities are client safety, the colleague’s safety, and objective documentation. Clients who received medications from her may have had errors and need reassessment, and she should not drive. Factual, timed observations go on the incident report. Writing about the impaired nurse in client charts is tempting because it seems thorough, but the chart holds client-care facts only and never refers to the incident report. Discussing her condition with the unit breaches confidentiality.
questions.takeaway: After removing an impaired nurse: reassess her clients, keep her from driving, and document facts on the incident report, not in the chart.
questions.hintContent: Who might have been harmed this morning, and who might be harmed on the way home?
questions.hintStrategy: For follow-up SATA items, check where documentation belongs and who needs to know.

questions.stem: A nurse manager receives concerns about a nurse’s interactions with a 24-year-old client on a rehabilitation unit. Which behaviors by the nurse suggest a boundary violation? Select all that apply.
options: Briefly mentioning her own leg fracture to ease his fear of therapy
Giving the client extra privileges that other clients do not receive
Giving the client her personal cell phone number for texting
Sitting with the client while he calls his family after a hard session
Coming to the unit on her days off to visit the client
Telling the client, “Let’s keep this between us; the others wouldn’t understand”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A brief disclosure that helps the client is a boundary crossing, not a violation.
Correct. Favoritism signals a relationship serving the nurse’s needs.
Correct. Private contact outside professional channels serves a personal relationship.
Incorrect. Supportive presence within the nurse’s role meets the client’s need.
Correct. Off-duty visits suggest a personal relationship with the client.
Correct. Secrecy is a hallmark of boundary violations.
questions.rationale: A boundary violation serves the nurse’s needs and can harm or exploit the client; warning signs include private contact, off-duty visits, secrets, and special treatment. A boundary crossing is brief, helps the client, and returns to normal. The brief self-disclosure about a fracture is the most tempting to select because personal sharing sounds risky, but it is short and meets the client’s need. The nurse, not the client, is responsible for keeping the boundary.
questions.takeaway: Ask whose need is met: the client’s and brief is a crossing; the nurse’s, secret, or repeated is a violation.
questions.hintContent: For each behavior, ask whose need it meets and whether it is brief or ongoing.
questions.hintStrategy: Use a single test question across all options so you do not over-select by instinct.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing a new graduate nurse’s social media activity during orientation. Which actions by the new nurse follow professional social media guidelines? Select all that apply.
options: Reporting a coworker’s post that shows a client’s tattoo
Declining a friend request from a client currently on the unit
Posting “Rough night with the guy in bed 12,” without a name
Posting general hand-washing tips with no client information
Sharing a unit party photo with a client’s door sign visible
optionRationales: Correct. Reporting privacy breaches by others is a professional duty.
Correct. Friending current clients risks boundary and privacy problems.
Incorrect. A bed number and timing can identify the client.
Correct. General health education without client details is appropriate.
Incorrect. Any visible identifying detail is a privacy breach.
questions.rationale: Professional social media use means never posting anything that could identify a client, avoiding personal connections with clients, and reporting colleagues’ breaches. General health education and declining client friend requests are appropriate, and reporting a coworker’s identifying photo protects privacy. The bed-number post is tempting to accept because no name appears, but a bed number and date can identify someone. A door sign in the background of a party photo is still a breach, intended or not.
questions.takeaway: If any detail could identify a client, do not post it; removing the name is not enough.
questions.hintContent: Could anyone who knows the client recognize them from the post?
questions.hintStrategy: For privacy SATA items, scan each option for indirect identifiers such as room numbers, photos, and rare details.
