questions.stem: During home visits in North Carolina, a nurse encounters several situations. Which situations require the nurse to report directly to the county department of social services? Select all that apply.
options: A colleague who documented a home visit 2 hours late
A 5-year-old with loop-shaped bruises on his back and no explanation
An adult with an intellectual disability whose caregiver leaves her without food
A capable 70-year-old who decides to stop taking her statin
A 9-year-old who missed a well-child visit because of a parent’s work schedule
optionRationales: Incorrect. Late charting is an internal practice matter.
Correct. Patterned bruising without explanation is suspicious for abuse and must be reported.
Correct. A disabled adult who needs protective services must be reported.
Incorrect. A capable adult’s informed choice is not a reportable situation.
Incorrect. A single missed visit with a reasonable cause does not suggest maltreatment.
questions.rationale: Some reports go straight from the person with the suspicion to an outside agency. In North Carolina, anyone who suspects a child is abused or neglected, and anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services, must report to the county department of social services. A missed well-child visit is tempting to report because it involves a child, but one missed visit with a clear reason is not evidence of neglect. A capable adult’s choice and a colleague’s late charting are not protective-services matters.
questions.takeaway: Suspected child maltreatment and disabled adults needing protection are reported directly to social services by the person who suspects it.
questions.hintContent: Which situations involve a child or dependent adult who may be unsafe?
questions.hintStrategy: For mandatory reporting SATA items, look for a vulnerable person plus a sign of harm or neglect.

questions.stem: A 91-year-old resident of a long-term care facility who is alert and oriented tells the nurse that an aide slapped her hand and called her “a stubborn old woman” during last night’s care. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Reporting the allegation to the supervisor right away
Documenting her statements in her own words with date and time
Waiting to see whether another resident reports the same aide
Listening without judgment and thanking her for telling
Assessing her hand and overall condition for injury
Asking the aide to apologize to her at the start of the next shift
optionRationales: Correct. Abuse allegations go to the supervisor immediately.
Correct. Objective documentation of her words supports the investigation.
Incorrect. Delay leaves residents at risk.
Correct. A nonjudgmental response supports the resident and encourages reporting.
Correct. Her current safety and any injury are assessed first.
Incorrect. This exposes the resident to the alleged abuser and treats abuse as a misunderstanding.
questions.rationale: When a resident reports abuse by staff, the nurse listens without judgment, assesses for injury and current safety, documents the resident’s words objectively, and reports to the supervisor right away so the aide can be removed from her care and the event investigated. An apology meeting is tempting because it seems to resolve the conflict, but it places her back with the alleged abuser. Waiting for more reports leaves her and others at risk. Advanced age or dependence never makes a report less credible.
questions.takeaway: Abuse allegation: listen, assess, document the client’s words, and report to the supervisor at once.
questions.hintContent: Which actions protect her and preserve an accurate account?
questions.hintStrategy: For abuse SATA items, select listen, assess, document, report; reject options that mediate, confront, or wait.

questions.stem: After a staff in-service on reporting unsafe conduct, a nurse manager evaluates staff understanding. Which statements by staff nurses indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “If my charge nurse is the one who is impaired, I go to the next level up.”
“I should confront my coworker before I tell anyone else.”
“I’ll watch the coworker for a few shifts to be sure before I report.”
“The duty to report covers aides, therapists, and providers, not just nurses.”
“I can report suspected impairment without having proof.”
optionRationales: Correct. When the supervisor is involved, the nurse goes up the chain.
Incorrect. The first report goes to the supervisor, not the coworker.
Incorrect. Waiting for proof is an unsafe delay.
Correct. The duty applies to any health care worker.
Correct. Suspicion is enough; supervisors investigate.
questions.rationale: The duty to report unsafe, unethical, or unprofessional conduct covers anyone on the team, is triggered by suspicion rather than proof, and follows the chain of command, skipping a level when the supervisor is involved. Confronting the coworker first is the tempting wrong belief because it feels fair, but the first report goes to the supervisor. Watching for several shifts delays protection while clients remain at risk. These principles let the nurse act quickly without investigating.
questions.takeaway: Report suspicion about anyone to your supervisor, or the next level if the supervisor is involved; do not confront or wait.
questions.hintContent: Which statements match “anyone, suspicion, supervisor first”?
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation SATA items, check each statement against the core rule; any delay or confrontation is wrong.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing restraint and seclusion events on an inpatient psychiatric unit. Which events represent coercive use that must be reported as a rights violation? Select all that apply.
options: Seclusion of a client for refusing to attend group therapy
Restraint after a client refused to give a technician his snacks
Emergency restraint of a client punching a peer after de-escalation failed
Wrist restraints applied during shift change because staff were busy
Seclusion of a client threatening staff with a broken chair leg
optionRationales: Correct. Seclusion used as punishment for refusing is coercive.
Correct. Restraint that benefits staff is abuse and a boundary violation.
Incorrect. Imminent danger after less restrictive measures failed is an emergency use.
Correct. Restraint for staff convenience is a violation.
Incorrect. An immediate threat of violence is an emergency.
questions.rationale: Clients in mental health settings have the right to be free from restraint and seclusion except in an emergency involving imminent danger. Using these measures to punish, to make staff work easier, or to benefit staff is coercive and must be reported to the supervisor and protective agencies. The emergency situations are tempting to select because restraint always feels serious, but restraint for active violence after de-escalation fails is permitted. The deciding question is whether imminent danger existed.
questions.takeaway: Emergency restraint responds to imminent danger; restraint for punishment, convenience, or staff benefit is a reportable violation.
questions.hintContent: For each event, ask whether anyone was in immediate danger.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each option into “emergency” or “punishment or convenience” before selecting.

questions.stem: A nurse has reported a colleague’s suspected drug diversion to the nurse manager, who is beginning an investigation. Which actions by the reporting nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Refusing to cosign any waste the nurse did not personally witness
Reassessing pain in clients who received opioids from the colleague
Searching the colleague’s bag for missing medication vials
Writing down objective facts about what was observed, with dates
Asking other nurses to watch the colleague and report back
optionRationales: Correct. Cosigning only witnessed wastes prevents false records.
Correct. Clients may not have received their medication and need reassessment.
Incorrect. Searching belongings is investigation that belongs to managers and pharmacy.
Correct. Factual notes support the investigation.
Incorrect. Recruiting surveillance spreads confidential concerns and is not the nurse’s role.
questions.rationale: Once diversion is reported, the reporting nurse focuses on client safety and accurate records while supervisors and pharmacy investigate. Clients may have had unrelieved pain, so they are reassessed, and the nurse continues to cosign only wastes actually witnessed. Searching the colleague’s bag is tempting because it seems to help gather proof, but investigation is not the staff nurse’s role and can violate policy. Recruiting coworkers to watch spreads confidential concerns.
questions.takeaway: After reporting diversion: protect clients, keep honest records, and let supervisors investigate.
questions.hintContent: Which actions are about client care and honest records rather than detective work?
questions.hintStrategy: In reporting SATA items, reject any option that turns the staff nurse into an investigator.
